A word on France: From a country perspective, headline figures today show a much lower print in France (48.4) than elsewhere (Germany: 52.8; rest of euro area: 53.5). But we would also highlight, again, that simple correlations between PMIs and GDP growth show the threshold for expansion/contraction in France is not 50, rather 48. Inflation to rise across the region In Brazil, IPCA inflation interrupted three months of deceleration in September and exceeded the BCB's target range of 3.00% +/- 1.5pp after a brief relief of two months, landing at 4.58% y/y currently. While the latest monthly moves were influenced mainly by food and energy prices, core measures also suggest an interruption in recent improvement. For example, in today's mid- month IPCA-15 release, core inflation rose 0.31% m/m, from 0.34% in September, with the annual measure at 4.5% y/y, from 4.4% a month earlier and 4.3% in August. Specifically, core services are also once again on the rise, up 5.5% y/y in mid-October, from 5.0% two months earlier, with the more volatile 3mma saar metric jumping from 4.8% to 6.3% in the same period. We forecast 2026 IPCA inflation at 5.1% y/y, up from 4.3% in 2025, and, if our trajectory is correct, the IPCA will breach the ceiling of the BCB's target of 3.0% +/-1.0pp again by running above 4.5% through February/March of next year. We still see important upside risks to our annual forecasts, especially 2027's 4.0%, due to disruptions from what is widely expected to be a very strong El Niño, possibly leading to challenging weather conditions that could affect food and electricity prices. Polling stations are generally open from 07:00 to 20:00. Seats are allocated under the d'Hondt method with a 3% electoral threshold, while minority lists are exempt. Polls point to a tight and uncertain race7 . Ruling SNS, which won 46.75% in 2023, was at 48.6% in the September Faktor Plus poll versus 37.1% for the Student List8 . The latest Ipsos poll conducted on 20-22 October has SNS at 47.4% versus 40% for the Student List, with an error margin of around 2pp based on decided voters9 . A poll of polls conducted by Poliwave.com as of 23 October shows ruling SNS support at 44.4% vs. the opposition at 41.7%. SPS is polling around 3-5% in most surveys and could become a kingmaker if SNS and the Student List finish close in terms of seats. While not guaranteed, SPS would appear more likely to form a coalition with SNS given their history of governing together since 2012. After polls close at 20:00 local time on Sunday, exit polls and initial projections should emerge between 20:00 and 21:00, followed by partial Official Electoral Council (RIK) vote counts between 21:00 and 23:00. Unless the race is extremely close, there should be a reasonably clear picture of the final result by late Sunday or early Monday.

The CME-LCH basis is likely to compress moving forward as rates decline because of directionality as well as the asymmetric convexity bias toward lower rates. The CME-LCH basis has returned as a topic of market discussion following its recent widening to levels that are only somewhat below historic highs. Lastly, the reduction in leveraged demand for funding in repo for relative value and basis trades has increased the amount of cash available that can be deployed to arbitrage dislocations in spreads. Collectively, these have made swap spreads more resilient to shocks. Rate rallies and equity sell-offs have exerted less tightening pressure on spreads than they would have historically. In addition, the equity sell-off this month was likely not large enough to trigger significant receiving flows in swaps to tighten spreads. SPX has been largely range-bound since end-July and is just off its recent highs, while the VIX is still just around 20. records.text: US Rates Weekly 23 October 2026 Citi Research 7 tracked the market’s expectation for policy rate changes (Figure 10), which makes intuitive sense given that an inactive/(active) Fed should be a headwind/(tailwind) for implied vol. But after this week’s risk off rate rally, a modest divergence has appeared with 3m2y implied vol moving higher while the pace of Fed hikes has been reduced. The relative richness of 3m2y vol is also apparent versus 3m5y vol, where the 3m5y/3m2y vol ratio looks slightly too low when compared against the 2s5s curve’s directionality to rates (Figure 11). Intuitively, a high directionality between the 2s5s curve and rate (more likely to bull flatten/bear steepen) should be reflected by a relatively higher implied vol on the 5y given that the long-end of the curve would be expected to lead. Currently, the 3m5y/3m2y vol ratio looks too low on this metric which speaks to the attractiveness of the conditional bull flattener. Argentina offers one such example. The Milei administration received substantial U.S. political and financial support dur- ing a period of acute volatility ahead of the October 2025 midterms. Its subsequent electoral victory reinforced expecta- tions of continued U.S. backing and gave the administration greater political room to pursue tax, labor and other structural reforms. The relationship thus became part of the broader sta- bilization story rather than merely a foreign-policy issue. Still, in the geopolitical arena, Colombia offered almost the mirror image. Relations with Washington had deteriorated sharply under President Petro, and foreign policy became an explicit dividing line in the election. De la Espriella cam- paigned on restoring close cooperation with the United States, particularly on security and counter-narcotics policy. His vic- tory therefore could represent not only a domestic policy shift but also a prospective geopolitical realignment. This could also be the case for Brazil if Bolsonaro retains his lead and secures the presidency by the end of the month. Clearly, this is particularly painful for economies already facing weak fiscal positions, where policymakers have little wiggle room to cushion households without adding to concerns around debt. The backdrop is made more challenging by the fact that higher oil is colliding with still resilient demand. The AI led investment cycle continues to support capex and keep demand for capital unusually strong. Rather than softer activity offsetting the inflationary impulse from energy, resilient growth and elevated credit issuance are reinforcing pressure on credit markets, raising the risk that central banks have to tighten further. Capex is expected to remain firm, supported by demand for labor-saving investment to address labor shortages and high corporate profits. records.text: Index exits matter more in HY than in IG For each month between January 2019 and September 2026, we identify bonds exiting the Bloomberg US Corporate Bond IG and HY indices. We then calculate monthly turnover, defined as TRACE trading volume divided by the amount outstanding at the time of exit, from six months before to six months after the exclusion date. The results are averaged across all exits in the sample, although the findings are broadly consistent over time. HY liquidity falls, IG liquidity remains resilient Turnover rises sharply around IG index exclusions, increasing from roughly 5% in the six months leading up to the exit to nearly 14% in the month of exclusion, likely reflecting repositioning around index changes (Figure 1). Trading activity then normalises but remains relatively resilient. Three months after leaving the index, average bond turnover is still around 4%, only modestly below pre-exit levels. We also observe a spike in turnover when bonds leave the Bloomberg US Corporate HY index, though much less pronounced than for IG (Figure 2). The key difference emerges after exclusions, when liquidity deteriorates significantly. Average turnover falls from around 9% before exit to roughly 5% afterwards, a decline of almost 50%. FIGURE 1. Against this backdrop, the key focus next week will be what guidance the BoJ provides regarding its assessment of underlying inflation and the criteria it uses to judge the pace and timing of rate hikes. The BoJ will likely use the Outlook Report to present staff analysis that clarifies how it assesses underlying inflation and to reduce differences in interpretation among Board members. Based on this analysis, the BoJ is expected to communicate the view that the 2% inflation target has been achieved. The BoJ may also explain the framework the BoJ uses to evaluate financial conditions, which would help markets assess the likely pace of tightening and the potential terminal rate. The case for the BoJ’s hawkish shift is reinforced by the September CPI report, which indicates that underlying inflation has clearly turned upward and broadened across both goods and services. We expect inflation to remain on an upward path, with the global core (ex. food and energy) measure projected to reach 3.0% in 1Q27, as pass-through from higher costs continues to feed into consumer prices. On growth, while September export volumes declined and posed some downside risk to 3Q GDP via net trade, the broader momentum still looks positive, supported by resilient global goods demand. More

managed We see greater tolerance for gradual CNY appreciation, rather than an objective of engineering a substantially stronger currency. Appreciation of around 3-4% is being characterised as manageable and USDCNY around 6.5-6.6 as conceivable. China’s competitiveness is reflecting manufacturing scale, supply-chain depth and intense domestic competition, suggesting that moderate CNY strength need not fundamentally undermine exports. A stronger CNY could support rebalancing by raising household purchasing power and lowering import costs, but rapid appreciation brings risks around manufacturing and capital flows. CNY internationalisation provides a more structural source of support, but greater trade settlement alone is insufficient. Foreign investors need deeper and more liquid CNY assets in which to recycle those balances, increasing the importance of CNH and government bond market development. The main constraint is capital-account sequencing: domestic outflows could respond rapidly to greater liberalisation, while foreign inflows may take longer to materialise. At the same time, weak credit demand reduces the effectiveness of conventional rate cuts and shifts more of the burden towards targeted monetary tools and fiscal policy. Taken together, the discussions suggest that gradual CNY appreciation can coexist with easier domestic policy, but the currency adjustment is likely to remain managed rather than develop into a one-way move. records.text: US Economics Weekly 23 October 2026 ab 3 US Economics Weekly UBS Research Economic Comment: more work to do We expect the FOMC to vote 10-2 to leave the target range for the federal funds rate unchanged at the October FOMC meeting. In the press conference, we expect Chairman Warsh’s message to be, essentially, ‘we have more work to do’. We expect he notes that in between the meetings the FOMC can watch and evaluate financial markets and the economic data, and fall back on his now typical ‘it’s the trend not the data point’ abstraction from the high frequency ebb and flow of data, markets and other events. We expect two dissents, one from Beth Hammack and one from Lorie Logan. We would not be surprised if there were only one dissent, or three. After skipping the October FOMC meeting, we expect the FOMC to raise rates by 0.25 pp at the December and January FOMC meetings. We expect the FOMC's decision to skip October reflects two things, one is the proximity of the mid-term elections and the second is the nature of the inflation problem that the FOMC faces. The problem is not rising inflation, nor an overheating economy. The problem is that 3% inflation is not headed toward 2% sufficiently fast. If inflation were more persistently rising and pressure mounting, there would be more urgency to raise rates in October too. records.text: US Economics Weekly 23 October 2026 ab 6 Updating our fiscal projections We updated our fiscal projections for the coming years to take on board the recent rise in interest rates and the implications for net interest expenses for the Federal government. We have written about these risks in recent weeks, see page 7 of this US Economics Weekly. Taking on board the new yield targets from US Rate Strategy, see here, we expect that this could add significantly to deficits in the coming years. The CBO expected net interest expenses to run roughly $1.1 trillion in FY 2027 and then ramp up by ~$100 billion per year after that. Those figures assumed a 10-year yield of 4.3%. We expect with the move higher in interest rates we could see additional interest expense of ~$140bn in 2027, $180bn in 2028, and ~$190bn in 2029. With this net interest expense could be running ~$1.5 trillion by FY 2029 or 4% of GDP, and the deficit would be running over 6.5% of GDP in the coming years, reaching 6.9% by 2029. We have also nudged up our expectations for spending in the coming years given the potential implications of increased Democratic control of Congress post-midterms. We expect that whether we see a divided government or a blue sweep the negotiations required in Congress around the budget process would lead to more not less spending. With these updates, we still expect that the fiscal impulse to growth flips from adding around 0.3pp to growth in 2026 in Q4/Q4 terms to subtracting -0.2pp in 2027

records.text: wer long-end Treasury supply has also supported spreads; we expect the Treasury to keep auction sizes unchanged at the November refunding, but tweak guidance to preserve flexibility and timing • Despite these near-term supportive factors, fiscal deficits and the longer-run Treasury supply outlook remain a structural force arguing for tighter long-end spreads in the medium term. While spreads may be less vulnerable, they are not immune to larger shocks. Long-end swap spreads have been resilient in recent months and spread volatility has been benign (Figure 1 and Figure 2). While spreads widened alongside the rise in yields, they have not retraced even as long-end rates fell from decade highs. Notably, the sell-off in equities tied to worries about the AI ecosystem and growth concerns did little to pressure spreads lower. Increased balance sheet capacity, Treasury buybacks and benign funding conditions have moderated the moves in risk-off episodes. At the same time, corporate pre-hedging activity tied to AI financing needs has provided support as borrowers compete for capital. In the current environment, we believe the hurdle for long-end spreads to tighten has increased and the transmission mechanism appears weaker. However, fiscal deficits and elevated Treasury borrowing needs remain the dominant driver for spreads, and they are not immune to larger risk-off moves that could tighten spreads. Applying this framework to our global food-price scenarios suggests that food inflation could add around 20bp to Canadian headline CPI by late 2027, with further effects extending into 2028. Transmission is gradual: weather shocks first affect crops, harvests, and exportable supply, before reaching global commodity prices and eventually domestic retail prices. The persistence of the energy shock increases the likelihood that these pressures reach consumers. Previously, we expected the pickup in food inflation to coincide with a substantial decline in energy prices over the second half of 2027, providing an offset to higher food costs. We now expect energy prices to remain elevated for longer, allowing cost pressures to accumulate and pass through successive stages of the food supply chain. The shift in the energy bottleneck toward refining, particularly diesel, exposes Canadian agriculture directly through farming equipment, transportation and distribution, while higher freight costs raise the prices of both domestically produced and imported food. Our input-output analysis also highlights the importance of transportation, processing, storage, and refrigeration in final food expenditure, suggesting that a prolonged energy shock can affect several stages of the supply chain simultaneously. records.text: olds directly own 42% of the US equity market and control the majority including indirect ownership via investment funds. The top 10% of households by wealth own 87% of total household equity assets. Federal Reserve data suggest that households bought $840 billion of US equities in H1 2026, more than offsetting a decline in net equity demand from US corporates. Higher-frequency mutual fund and ETF flows show continued strong demand in recent months. Going forward, the trajectory of the labor market and interest rates will be n key determinants of household equity demand, which in turn will help determine the near- and long-term path of US equities. Household equity demand is sensitive to employment, wealth, and the competition from yields on cash and bonds. Our baseline forecasts suggest household demand will remain solid in 2027, although recent macro volatility is a reminder of the risks around those forecasts. Looking further ahead, a secular shift in retirement asset allocation is a tailwind for equity demand, while interest rates and AI-related disruption are key sources of uncertainty. Of course, a model built solely on oil market fundamentals cannot capture every movement in prices. Uncertainty can push prices away from fair value, sometimes by a wide margin. During the COVID pandemic, crude traded at a discount of nearly $20/bbl to our model’s estimated value. In the first months following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, prices carried a premium of roughly $15. Deviations of this magnitude make forecasting oil prices considerably more difficult, even when the underlying supply and demand outlook is relatively clear. But before we attribute today’s nearly $20 gap entirely to geopolitics, we need to ask whether something else has changed in the way oil is being priced. One reason to question this explanation is the growing divergence in physical crude markets. Crude grades that once moved broadly in line with benchmark prices are now trading at sharply different levels. With freight costs reaching extraordinary highs, the key question is whether transportation costs are merely widening physical price differentials or whether they are also influencing the benchmarks against which these barrels are priced. The scale of the divergence in physical crude prices is striking. So far in October, the UAE’s Upper Zakum crude price has averaged just $71/bbl, Congo’s Djeno $79 and Brazil’s Mero $89. The broad-based price pressures embedded within the CPI print appear to underline the breadth of inflationary pressures facing the economy, a clear focus of Chairman Warsh. Yet we doubt that the FOMC would proceed with a hike. Recent communications from FOMC members have pushed back against October hike expectations. With the market pricing the probability of a hike sitting below 10% at the time of publication, the Fed would be seen to deliver a strongly hawkish hike if it did hike. This could add further volatility to the market, which could be construed as political a few days before US midterm elections. We expect two hawkish dissents, from Presidents Hammack and Logan, with some risk that Kashkari or Waller joins them. With core inflation still contained and the labor-market signal uneven, we think the Bank can afford to assess the incoming evidence after an initial adjustment. Clearer broadening in underlying inflation would bring the second hike forward; renewed weakness in demand would argue for greater patience. We also expect that, given existing excess supply in the economy, the Bank will not need to hike further. We therefore expect a measured 50bp recalibration to a more persistent inflation outlook, not the start of a sustained tightening cycle. Most of the tightening has come from the increase in long-term yields, but concerns around France have also led sovereign spreads to widen and equities to re-rate lower. Our analysis finds that the recent tightening of conditions could subtract 0.1-0.5% from real GDP using two ECB measures of financial conditions and 0.2% using our own index. ECB commentary has been quite balanced, emphasising that a “measured approach” to policy tightening remains appropriate. In particular, ECB speakers have noted ongoing inflation risks, but also highlighted that inflation pressures have so far not broadened and that tighter financial conditions will slow growth, potentially substituting for rate tightening. ECB officials have said little about sovereign risk. A Hold Next Week The Governing Council is widely expected to stay on hold next week given the recent emphasis on a “measured pace” of adjustment. As usual, investors will look to the Monetary Policy Statement and Q&A for signals about the future policy path. Starting with the statement, we expect no changes to the formal policy language, with the Council likely to reiterate that it will set policy using a data-dependent and meeting-by-meeting approach. ECB officials are likely to maintain their risk assessment, with upside risks to inflation and downside risks to growth. We do not look for significant changes to the description of the incoming data

We think he would be asked how staying on hold after the strong September inflation data is consistent with his prior comment that “inflation is a choice”. Warsh will probably say that he’s focused on trends rather than individual data points. But this is a difficult case to make without sounding complacent on inflation, given that those same trends (which have now been revised down a bit) led the Fed to hike in Sep. Especially if Warsh isn’t willing to lock in a Dec increase by guiding the markets toward a quarterly pace of hikes. In one sense, the hurdle for intervening with TPI is high. The TPI can only address unwarranted or non -fundamental risk premia . France has weak fiscal fundamentals and ultimately the exit from this episode of stress requires investor confidence in a credible path back to fiscal sustainability. That needs the 2027 Budget to pass without significant slippage and RN’s journey toward s fiscal orthodoxy to continue. Neither can be blown off course by social unrest. With the election still six months away, the elevated political risk premia are going to linger. If something needs to happen, maybe French banks’ low exposure to OATs could act as an initial buffer to absorb market pressure. At the same time, the ECB will be watching the speed at which the market is moving. The TPI was created to address unwarranted and disorderly market conditions. A market that is moving too quickly and is becoming dysfunctional could lower the hurdle for intervention. The ECB won’t tolerate irrational pricing, one-way markets, liquidity spirals or flight to quality dynamics. The ECB wants to maintain the disciplining role of the market but has no interest in the market breaking. records.text: M Idea 2 Headline Higher, Core Stable Our EA October inflation forecasts | Headline slightly up and core stable: October could bring just a slight uptick of headline inflation at 3.9%Y, from 3.8%Y in September. The increase in energy year-on-year inflation could be limited this month (19.7%Y from 18.9%Y) as fuel prices could fall on the back of policy measures in Germany and Spain. However, higher wholesale natural gas prices should continue to feed through to retail gas and electricity tariffs. The September upside surprise for food inflation was due to volatile vegetable prices and we assume vegetable prices will partly reverse their September increase this month. Still, base effects from a soft Oct-25 could yield a slight increase in the annual food inflation rate (1.4%Y from 1.3%Y). For core, we foresee a stable print at 2.5%Y. Goods inflation could move up (1.3%Y from 1.1%Y) but it remains dominated by idiosyncratic factors in IT-products ("chipflation") and lubricants (which is part of goods as per Eurostat classification). Services inflation is forecast stable (3.2%Y). We see upside risks from tourism-related items, but disinflation could continue in the rest of the services basket. Higher gasoline futures prices, persistent refining bottlenecks, and the scheduled normalization of fuel excise taxes account for much of the upward revision. • The energy shock is increasingly becoming a core inflation risk. As discussed in our recent global inflation deep dive, energy shocks that persist for two to three quarters increasingly transmit through transportation, logistics, agriculture, and intermediate inputs. We expect pass-through to begin picking up in 4Q26 and accelerate in 1Q27, taking underlying inflation toward 2.4%. • Other inflation pressures are accumulating. Our food-price models suggest that higher global prices could add around 20bp to headline inflation by late 2027, while semiconductor-related price increases could contribute another 10–20bp. records.text: M Idea 10 Financial conditions: The Fed awakens Following the 25bp rate hike in September and the shift into an "oil risk premium" baseline, we reset our financial conditions index to September 15, 2026, the day prior to the September FOMC meeting, to track our FRB/US-based measure of financial conditions in this new hiking cycle. As of the October 22nd market close, financial conditions were 22bp tighter than they were before the September FOMC meeting. The index aims to capture how changes in asset prices weigh on future economic activity. It includes five daily variables: the 10-year Treasury yield, S&P 500 returns, the corporate BBB credit spread, the valuation of the U.S. dollar, and the price of oil. These are aggregated based on their estimated growth elasticities relative to the federal funds rate using the Federal Reserve's FRB/US model. As a result, the index can be interpreted as the equivalent change in the federal funds rate, expressed in basis points, required to generate a similar effect on economic activity. From the day before the September FOMC meeting until October 22, the tightening in financial conditions has been equivalent to about a 22bp hike in the federal funds rate, reflecting dollar appreciation. The FCI had been tighter a week earlier, on October 15; and it tightened further through most of this week, until it reversed course with a drop in 10- year Treasury yields on October 22. Higher freight costs are being absorbed partly through lower FOB prices— particularly for barrels traveling longer distances—while refiners still face sharply higher delivered costs (Figure 7). The result is a market in which crude can become more expensive for the buyer even as it becomes less valuable to the producer. But does this explain why Brent is trading nearly $20 above its fundamental value? Our analysis suggests not. Despite the extraordinary increase in freight costs, we find no evidence of material freight pass-through into either Brent futures or Dated Brent. The adjustment is occuring primarily through physical crude differentials, rather than through the benchmarks themselves. This leaves geopolitical risk as the more plausible explanation for Brent’s premium over fair value. Geography is reshaping the relative value of crude around the world, but it does not explain why the benchmark itself remains so elevated. The distinction matters: one reflects the cost of moving oil today. The other reflects what the market is willing to pay for the possibility that tomorrow’s supply may once again be disrupted. Russian Urals has traditionally been priced on both a free-on-board (FOB) basis at Russian export terminals—where the buyer covers delivery costs—and on a delivered basis, including cost, insurance and freight (CIF) at destination ports—where the producer pays the expenses. Historically, however, it made little difference to the overall crude price: freight from Russia to Europe was typically only around $2 per barrel. Since Western sanctions redirected Russian exports toward Asia, opaque shipping arrangements, intermediary margins and sanctions-related costs have made it increasingly difficult to determine how much producers actually receive. Most Middle Eastern crudes are assessed through yet another mechanism. Saudi grades, Iraq’s Basrah and Kuwait Export Crude are more commonly sold under term contracts using official selling prices (OSPs). Rather than negotiating a fixed outright price for each cargo, producers typically set a monthly premium or discount to a regional benchmark—generally Oman/Dubai for Asian buyers, and often Dated Brent (or a related Brent reference) for European buyers. Uncertainty can push prices away from fair value, sometimes by a wide margin. During the COVID pandemic, crude traded at a discount of nearly $20/bbl to our model’s estimated value. In the first months following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, prices carried a premium of roughly $15. Deviations of this magnitude make forecasting oil prices considerably more difficult, even when the underlying supply and demand outlook is relatively clear. But before we attribute today’s nearly $20 gap entirely to geopolitics, we need to ask whether something else has changed in the way oil is being priced. One reason to question this explanation is the growing divergence in physical crude markets. Crude grades that once moved broadly in line with benchmark prices are now trading at sharply different levels. With freight costs reaching extraordinary highs, the key question is whether transportation costs are merely widening physical price differentials or whether they are also influencing the benchmarks against which these barrels are priced. The scale of the divergence in physical crude prices is striking. So far in October, the UAE’s Upper Zakum crude price has averaged just $71/bbl, Congo’s Djeno $79 and Brazil’s Mero $89. records.text: See Appendix A-1 for Analyst Certification, Important Disclosures and Research Analyst Affiliations. 23 Oct 2026 15:46:23 ET │ 18 pages Canada Economics Weekly On hold CITI'S TAKE We expect the Bank of Canada to leave policy rates unchanged at 2.25% on Wednesday despite markets pricing around 20bp of a hike. Recent data, including a decline in core inflation measures back below 2% in September CPI data on Monday, have not met the conditions outlined for officials to conclude that rates necessarily need to be higher to control inflation. Communications should still sound hawkish, as officials would not hesitate to raise rates if there is evidence of higher energy costs pushing up other prices. In our base case, notable inflation pass-through does not occur. Soft demand, with still-low indications of significant capacity constraints in the Q3 BOS, should continue to counteract upward pressures from higher input costs, keeping core inflation around target and rates unchanged this year. Policy rate pricing, in contrast, is meaningfully more hawkish than our economists’ forecasts across regions. We think this relative picture is consistent with a US front end that reflects a more hawkish Fed reaction function than our economists expect, whereas in Europe and the UK the discrepancy comes down more clearly to a divergence of inflation views. That setup is more favorable for real rate longs in the US, where a benign relaxation in inflation pressures can see real rates outperform their typical relationship with nominals. In Europe, it argues more for short inflation exposure, either outright or via nominal longs, given richer inflation pricing relative to both our economists’ forecasts and model-implied fair value. Lower realized inflation should also support a return to steeper inflation curves in the Euro area and the UK. There was also a large and unexpected drop in the ILO unem- ployment rate to 4.7%. This message was reinforced by the rise in the employment PMI, as mentioned above. The PMI’s output price reading showed a surprise fall, but we look to next week’s DMP survey to get a cross-check on whether businesses are struggling to pass on higher costs (we assume they won’t struggle, and look for a rise in DMP pricing inten- tions next week). Pressure on the BoE to keep tightening The combination of higher inflation, a strengthening labour market and resilient growth places greater pressure on the BoE to raise rates. A November hike is assured, but we do not yet think the data will push the MPC to tighten policy at con- secutive meetings this year (i.e. in November and December). The lack of second-round effects to date means the MPC will probably skip December. And renewed concerns about the pace of consumption in the coming months – amplified by the drop in Gfk consumer confidence and retail sales this week – also provides further grounds for caution. Nevertheless, our new inflation profile stays high in 2Q as well, reflecting the shape of the energy market curves. Assuming growth holds up, we therefore see increased risk

With most of the FOMC already on board with two hikes this year and the inflation data looking more problematic, we think the latter option is more valuable for the Fed. Who’s really in charge? Water levels in the hydroelectric dams keep falling, approaching critical levels that could force the government to implement rationing. As of October 22, the Mazar reservoir reached 2122.7 m.a.s.l., just 6.7 meters from the critical level. If the trend of the last two months holds, the critical level could be reached within the next 15 days. The government so far has been trying to avoid widespread blackouts, instead intensifying restrictions for large industrial consumers, which have been asked to disconnect from the power grid up to three days a week and rely on self-generation during those periods, but it is unclear if this would be sufficient to contain the decline in the reservoir. The government subsequently reissued the same adjustment through a transitional decree, and in July the court lifted the suspension, holding that the law does not prescribe a mathematical formula but instead requires that the relevant factors be considered and justified. The evidentiary stage closed in late September, Fenalco submitted its closing argu- ments in October, and a ruling on the merits has yet to be issued. For 2026 wages, the case is now largely academic. Historical precedent suggests that any annulment would apply prospec- tively, as occurred in 2017 with the 2016 decree, without trig- gering a recalculation of wages already paid. The key issue is therefore the timing and reasoning of the final decision. A rul- ing before December that follows the February logic would require the government to more explicitly demonstrate the weight assigned to each statutory factor, making another increase driven primarily by living-wage considerations more difficult to defend. By contrast, a ruling closer to the court's July reasoning would preserve greater discretion for the administration. records.text: United Kingdom The flash composite PMI accelerated to 53.1, up from 52.0 in September, coming in above our expectation (51.9) and the Bloomberg consensus (51.7) (Figure 7). The increase in the composite output was driven by both services activity (+1.0pt to 53.1) and manufacturing output (+1.6pt to 53.1) expanding. The headline manufacturing index (a weighted composite of the five subindices) accelerated by 0.9pt to 52.8, less than output due to a contraction in employment. The October PMIs continue to show resilient activity in the face of increased energy costs. The press release cited demand conditions were buoyed by increased sales from AI investment and increased demand for technology services, alongside robust global economic conditions. Some firms continue to express concern over future headwinds from geopolitical uncertainty and weak consumer confidence. Strong growth in technology services is consistent with recent GDP data, which have pointed to strong investment in the ICT sector, and robust output growth in the professional services sector. Input prices for services (+0.1pt to 69.3) and manufacturing (+3.1pt to 71.5) firms both rose again in October. Interestingly, even with more resilient activity, the PMIs continue to suggest margins are being compressed (Figure 8). records.text: ies this week – led by Meta – could have calmed markets. Meta's earnings on Wednesday initially did the trick: Q3 exceeded expectations and the market rallied. However, Meta also presented yet another upward revision to its capex forecasts (to $135-145bn). It plans to fund this by the issuance of a new class of non-voting shares,1 while also posting a deficit of $2.1bn in free cash flow, its first reported negative cash flow in more than a decade. Investors started to have second thoughts. These factors raised fresh concerns about the durability of the AI investment cycle. As a consequence, despite strong earnings, Meta stock dropped 7% on Thursday, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq was down 3.2% at the time of publication. Earnings alone no longer suffice, with investors becoming increasingly vigilant about the broader AI investment narrative. The many key AI earnings reports coming in next week – Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon, Intel, SK Hynix, and Samsung are all reporting – should provide further evidence of whether the AI angst of recent weeks continues or eventually subsides again, as it has in the past. However, if Meta is any guide, simply showing strong earnings may no longer be enough. records.text: Inflation pricing looks about fair in the US but slightly rich in Europe Easing tariff- and AI-related price pressures, alongside lower commodity prices, should support more benign headline and core inflation in the US and Europe in 2027. Our US economists think the inflationary effects of tariffs are largely behind us and the impact of AI demand is near its peak, while the outlook for shelter inflation should support a more benign path for core inflation. Our commodities strategists also expect improving energy supply to push oil and natural gas prices lower over the next 12 months, easing headline inflation globally. There are clear upside risks, however, particularly if energy-market disruptions intensify. Market pricing is broadly consistent with our economists’ US inflation path through the end of 2027 but somewhat elevated relative to their European forecasts for next year (Exhibit 3). A key driver of the more benign Euro Area outlook is our commodities strategists’ expectation of a faster normalization in energy prices, particularly European diesel, petrol spreads, and TTF. Substituting market forwards for those assumptions removes much of the premium in traded inflation through mid-2027, but a gap persists further out. This may reflect expectations of stronger second-round effects or a higher inflation risk premium. records.text: are a key guide for further BoJ tightening The BoJ continues its hiking cycle based on the assessment that financial conditions remain accommodative. Recent Policy Board discussions suggest that rate hikes will continue as long as this remains the case. Conversely, if signs emerge that financial conditions are beginning to tighten meaningfully, the BoJ could slow the pace of hikes or reassess the terminal rate. At the post-September meeting press conference, Governor Ueda explained that financial conditions can be assessed through three channels: (1) interest rates, (2) bank lending, and (3) asset markets such as equities. While the BoJ sees a significant tightening in long-term interest rates, it continues to judge the latter two channels as accommodative. This assessment appears reasonable, in our view. Bank lending growth remains robust at 5.7%y/y, supported by demand related to real estate and M&A activity, while firms continue to characterize banks' lending attitudes as accommodative. The Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey released this week also showed a modest improvement in DI measures of loan demand from both firms and households over the past three months. The majority of banks still reported rising loan demand, with little evidence that recent increases in interest rates have materially weakened borrowing demand (see heatmap below). Expectations for the next three months are similarly stable, with no meaningful decline in demand anticipated.

Heading into the week, we thought the Governing Council could remain on hold next week if under- lying inflation stayed contained and the 3Q Business Outlook Survey and Canadian Survey of Consumer Expectations showed no evidence that inflation expectations were becom- ing unanchored. With the labor market still operating in excess supply, that combination would have allowed policy- makers to wait for clearer evidence that higher energy costs were spilling into broader prices before tightening policy. Only one of those conditions was met. The September CPI showed little evidence that higher energy costs were feeding into underlying inflation. The Bank’s preferred core measures eased to an average of 1.9%oya, while the exclusionary core held at 2.1%. However, the Canadian Survey of Consumer Expectations showed a material deterioration in longer-term consumer inflation expectations, with five-year expectations rising to 3.9% from 3.4% in 2Q (Figure 1). The Business Out- look Survey also indicated that firms expect to pass more of their recent cost increases on to customers, raising the risk that the current stability in core inflation will not persist. We expect CPI inflation in Tokyo to slow in October, with the CPI excluding perishables and energy (core-core) at +2.4% y/y, down from +3.0% in September, and CPI excluding perishables alone (core) at +2.4%, down from +2.7%. Although Tokyo CPI inflation rose sharply in September, the temporary boost from water charges – one of the main drivers – will fade. In addition, distribution of the new rice crop will gather pace from October, widening rice’s negative contribution (see above Rice set to exert greater downward pressure on CPI from October onward). Accommodation charges will likely also make a smaller contribution, partly reflecting base effects from last year’s price increases. For core inflation, higher electricity and city gas charges are expected to partially offset these downward pressures. We look for the unemployment rate to remain at 2.5% in September (August : 2.5%) as the structural and irreversible tightening of the labor market continues. 23 October 2026 21 Barclays | Market Strategy Japan: Standing pat while reaching 2%

We have held a received bias in Nov RBA for some time, predicated on our view that back-to-back rate hikes were unlikely (see EM Asia: What you need to know this week (28 Sep - 4 Oct), dated 28 September). While inflation remains elevated, other developments point towards softness in the economy. Consumer sentiment has fallen again following the RBA’s rate hike in September and are approaching decade lows (Figure 1), which is likely to further the ongoing housing market correction (Figure 2). On the labour market, although the latest unemployment rate falls within the RBA’s implicit 4.5–5.0% target range, it has continued to trend upwards (Figure 3). Coupled with the negative employment print in August, it suggests that monetary policy was already restrictive prior to the rate hike in September, supporting the argument for a pause in November. Softer trajectory: In fact, we believe risk–reward is more attractive to receive the November meeting at these levels. While Q3 CPI remains a risk, the inflation trajectory since the latest hike has been softer than market’s expectations, with both headline and trimmed-mean surprising to the downside in the August CPI print. There has also been a divergence between the quarterly and monthly trimmed-mean indices – the former rose by only 0.81% over Q2, compared to the 0.96% implied by its monthly counterpart (Figure 5) – something we think can happen again in Q3. The widest level that 10y CME LCH basis got to both during the 2018 widening episode and the 2021-22 episode when large imbalances were prevalent was between 3.0-3.5bp. After these episodes, the basis gradually corrected over the following 2-3 years. What is the outlook? Rates have begun to fall, and we are biased long duration. Lower rates shorten mortgage duration, reduce the need for mortgage-related paying and could lead to receiving as existing hedges are adjusted. Further, convexity hedging needs themselves are now likely biased to the downside (Figure 2). The September retail sales report showed some recent moderation in goods spending, but for 3Q as a whole, goods are tracking a strong +4.0% (q/q saar) and services are robust as well, +3.5%. A catch-up effect may be part of the story. A second likely candidate is the wealth effect, which has helped underpin spending by upper income households. Upper income households have an outsized share in most categories of durables spending. A third cause could be fiscal policy, where the 20% increase in tax refunds likely provided cushion exactly when households needed it. Finally, consumers do what consumers do during periods of stress; they draw on liquid resources and pull the saving rate lower to avoid large swings in spending. Finally, some of the strength in consumer spending in third quarter may be more statistical than real. Residual seasonality in inflation means that inflation tends to be higher in 1Q, which mechanically acts as a drag on real consumption growth. This pays back throughout the rest of the year, mostly in the second half. Recall that real consumption growth accelerated from 0.7% in 1Q 25 to 2.1% in the second quarter to 3.7% in the third quarter, only to slip back to 1.9% in the fourth quarter. Using a four-quarter change smooths through any seasonal distortion. Even our forecast for real consumption growth of 3.7% q/q saar in the third quarter – on the heels of a 3.8% rise in the second quarter – implies year-on-year growth of 2.6%.

records.text: Global Markets Strategy 23 October 2026 J P M O R G A N www.jpmorganmarkets.com Global Commodities Research Natasha Kaneva (1-212) 834-3175 natasha.kaneva@jpmorgan.com Lyuba Savinova (1-212) 270-3781 lyuba.savinova@jpmchase.com Artem Fakhretdinov (1-212) 272-1839 artem.fakhretdinov@jpmorgan.com JPMorgan Chase Bank NA What is the price of oil? Eight months into the war with Iran, what should be a straightforward question has become surprisingly hard to answer. Oil is once again flowing from the Middle East, and our pricing model puts Brent’s fair value at $94/ bbl. Yet Brent is trading near $114, almost $20 above what fundamentals imply. Is this simply the price of geopolitical risk, or is something else influencing the value of oil? We have never been fully comfortable with the concept of ‘geopolitical risk premium.’ Not because geopolitical risk is irrelevant, but because it is remarkably difficult to quantify. Over the years, we have tested conflict indicators, geopolitical risk indices, and even the performance of traditional safe-haven assets as explanatory variables in our oil pricing model. None improved the model’s fit. Moreover, any risk premium tends to be fleeting. Historically, sustained deviations of more than 5% above our model’s fair value have lasted on average just 3.8 months before prices either converged back to fundamentals or slipped into a discount. Of course, a model built solely on oil market fundamentals cannot capture every movement in prices. Uncerta

In 2027, we expect these pressures to fade, but think the resulting relief is likely to be traded differently across regions. In the US, price pressures have largely translated into higher real rates, while in n Europe and the UK they have had a more pronounced impact on traded inflation. Inflation pricing is broadly consistent with our economists’ forecasts for next year in the US, although it appears somewhat elevated in Europe. Our fair value models reinforce this: traded inflation is close to fair value across the US curve, but somewhat rich to model-implied levels in Europe, primarily through the front end of the curve. Markets are pricing more hawkish policy paths than our economists forecast n across regions. We think this relative picture is consistent with a US front end that reflects a more hawkish Fed reaction function than our economists expect, whereas in Europe and the UK the discrepancy comes down more clearly to a divergence of inflation views. With the presidential election scheduled for April 2027 and a runoff in May, the medium - term fiscal outlook remains highly uncertain. The leading candidates, Marine Le Pen and Mélenchon, are both critical of fiscal tightening, suggesting that campaign politics could further complicate consolidation efforts. While campaign pledges may soften after the election, the resulting adjustment is still likely to prove insufficient to reassure investors about France's debt trajectory. This leaves French government bonds vulnerable to political and fiscal headlines. One factor that could help contain market pressure is the possibility of ECB intervention. The ECB has developed several asset -purchase tools over the past decade. The Public Sector Purchase Program (PSPP), announced in 2015, was the centerpiece of quantitative easing and aimed at combating low inflation. The Pandemic Emergency Purchase Program (PEPP), introduced in 2020, was designed to address the economic shock from Covid. More recently, the ECB created the Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI) in 2022 as it began raising rates and became concerned that sovereign spreads could widen in a disorderly manner. Unlike PSPP and PEPP, which were monetary policy tools, TPI was ex plicitly designed to address fragmentation and spread widening. However, it is not unconditional. records.text: ook for food inflation Food and non-alcoholic beverages (FNAB) inflation held steady at 1.3% y/y in September, with the significant disinflation in food this year remaining intact (Figure 15). We think data outturns continue to validate a forecast for food that doesn't begin to pick up materially until the beginning of 2027 and peaks in the second half of the year, as the energy shock begins to push up consumer prices. As we have highlighted, recent increases in gas prices pose more inflationary risks to food than oil, and we remain wary of further increases in gas prices for future developments in food inflation. We continue to view El Niño as a risk to our forecast rather than a catalyst to materially adjust it, due to the lack of clarity on exact weather events and their subsequent impact on UK food inflation. Output prices for food accelerated in September, albeit from a very low base (+0.4pp to -0.6% y/y) (Figure 16). We think this is consistent with the gradual pick-up in food inflation expected in our forecast, and remain vigilant to the various upside risks that may lead to a quicker or stronger inflation of food products next year. We forecast FNAB inflation of 1.0% y/y in Dec-26 and 2.7% y/y in Dec-27. 23 October 2026 6 Barclays | UK inflation forecast update

records.text: 23 October 2026 Focus Europe Deutsche Bank AG Page 3 speech ECB Chief Economist Philip Lane described the tightening of financial conditions as “material”. What is needed to justify a further hike to 3% in March 2027: (1) Iran energy disruptions continue, (2) growth remains robust despite tighter financial conditions (the softer October PMI might signal that financial conditions are starting to bite, at least in France) , and – in particular – (3) clear evidence of second-round wage effects. This is not our baseline. Eight months into the war with Iran, what should be a straightforward question has become surprisingly hard to answer. Oil is once again flowing from the Middle East, and our pricing model puts Brent’s fair value at $94/ bbl. Yet Brent is trading near $114, almost $20 above what fundamentals imply. Is this simply the price of geopolitical risk, or is something else influencing the value of oil? We have never been fully comfortable with the concept of ‘geopolitical risk premium.’ Not because geopolitical risk is irrelevant, but because it is remarkably difficult to quantify. Over the years, we have tested conflict indicators, geopolitical risk indices, and even the performance of traditional safe-haven assets as explanatory variables in our oil pricing model. None improved the model’s fit. Moreover, any risk premium tends to be fleeting. Historically, sustained deviations of more than 5% above our model’s fair value have lasted on average just 3.8 months before prices either converged back to fundamentals or slipped into a discount. LLC Martin Tobias, CFA, CMT Martin.Tobias@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-6076 Matthew Hornbach, CMT Matthew.Hornbach@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-1863 Aryaman Singh Aryaman@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-1993 Eli Carter Eli.Carter@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-4703 October FOMC preview: set up for disappointment We think investors might still be operating under their tried and true frameworks that applied to how the Fed used to operate, prior to the change in leadership in June. Instead of taking their own view on how the incoming data had evolved relative to the dual mandate and how the Fed should react to that evolution, investors went into Chairman Warsh’s fireside chat in Thailand looking for an answer they were not likely to get (see Exhibit 1 ). As the saying goes, old habits die hard. This leaves market pricing for the October FOMC meeting susceptible to a surprise, since it’s the trends that matter in the mind of Chairman Warsh – and the inflation trend has not improved since the summer, as our economists note. If the Fed were to deliver a surprise hike, we think that would continue the trend of repricing the risk of additional hikes lower in the medium term (see Exhibit 2 ). Monthly GDP in August was much weaker than expected, contracting -0.04% y/y versus a 1.5% expansion expected by the consensus. This print is the result of a combination of that month's earthquake impact and the deceleration of fiscal expenditures. The former might be a temporary effect that could revert over the coming months but the latter is likely to become increasingly relevant. This week President De La Espriella announced a COP13.8trn (USD4.3bn or c. 0.7% of GDP) in fiscal spending cuts. This is part of the adjustment that was announced in August when the revised 2027 budget was presented. De La Espriella said this is “just the beginning” of a process intended to put the public finances in order. The announcement is a positive signal that could mark the prelude for the presentation of the fiscal adjustment plan, better known as the Rescue Bill, which is expected for next week and should bring additional fiscal tightening measures that would enter into effect from 2027 onwards. Considering that the root of Colombia’s inflation problem has been an excessively loose fiscal policy, the move towards a tighter fiscal policy should complement the tightening already made from the monetary policy side (300bp YTD), containing additional inflation pressures and balancing risks such as El Niño or pressures from higher fuel prices. In this regard, the BoJ’s October 2026 Financial System Report, released on 23 October, presented an analysis of the impact of higher interest rates on firms and households. Areas warranting attention include the wide variation in financial conditions among firms with net debt and, for households, rising loan sizes driven primarily by higher property prices, alongside an increase in ultra-long-term mortgages with maturities exceeding 35 years. In H1 2026, Federal Reserve data show that public and private US corporates issued $175 billion of US equities on net. Including expiring lockups, we expect the net supply of US public equity will increase next year by the largest amount since 2000. Household demand will be crucial to balance this supply. The trajectory of the labor market and interest rates will help determine the strength of household demand for equities in 2027. During the past few decades, flows into US equity mutual funds and ETFs have generally improved following increases in household net worth, decreases in unemployment, and declines in the perceived risk of recession. Equity flows have also been inversely correlated with changes in the yield offered by cash and bonds. Our economists’ baseline outlook for 2027 embeds a stable labor market and modest declines in yields, which should be supportive for continued household equity demand. INTERNATIONAL PLC Fabio Bassanin, CFA Fabio.Bassanin@morganstanley.com +44 20 7425-1869 UK Budget Preview Recent price action and positioning suggest that market expectations have become increasingly constructive ahead of the Budget Gilt yields remain historically elevated and at the top of the peer range (see Exhibit 1), largely reflecting higher front-end yields. Beneath the surface, however, UK duration has performed relatively well more recently. Following initial underperformance in the wake of the US–Iran conflict, 10-year gilts have since rallied more strongly than most G7 peers, increasingly trading in line with core markets and exhibiting more pronounced safe-haven characteristics, a somewhat unusual development by recent historical standards (Exhibit 2). Notably, the recent widening in EGB spreads has generated limited spillovers into gilts. The UK's relatively favorable fiscal outlook may have provided some support, with the IMF recently singling out the UK for its fiscal consolidation plans, in contrast to other major economies facing persistent borrowing pressures. This divergence may have helped compress UK fiscal risk premia and limit spillover from sovereign markets facing renewed fiscal concerns. India was the biggest official buyer of long-term USTs in August at $16bn (z- score of 3.2). This was after purchasing $15bn in July. India has sold about $50.6bn long-term USTs in 2025 as they were trying to fight the cheapening of INR vs the dollar. With the currency finally stabilizing in recent months, they are likely to replenish their dollar assets. The $49bn T-Bill sales from Japan were also mostly official. As a reminder, Japan intervened to strengthen their currency at the tail end of July, where settlement would have rolled into August. As of the end of August, Japan drained most of their T-bill holdings and now sit at around $30bn left from a peak of ~$150bn (Figure 18). Figure 20. Turning to the positives, wages come first. Through August, scheduled cash earnings maintained y/y growth of 3% or more for eight consecutive months. By this time of year, the reflection of shunto base-pay increases into scheduled cash earnings is normally largely complete. Second, the September Tankan showed an improvement in the manufacturing business conditions DI for both large and small firms, led by global AI-related demand, while the non-manufacturing DI remained elevated ( Figure 2). Focus IMF takeaways: Postcard from Bangkok EM Asia growth remains resilient, despite rising geopolitical, inflation and El Niño risks. Fund flows have remained stable with no major visible signs of stress. There is growing agreement that the Asia trade is about differentiation. This article was originally published on 20 October 2026. The IMF argues that the global economy remains remarkably resilient despite multiple shocks, with stable growth, resilient labour markets and easing inflation. However, it warns that geopolitical risks, supply disruptions and higher-for-longer rates leave economies vulnerable, underscoring the need to rebuild fiscal and monetary policy buffers. The IMF forecasts global growth of 2.5% in 2026 and 2.8% in 2027, with EMs, led by Asia, remaining the main engine of growth. While we broadly agree on China, we are more optimistic on overall growth due to our view of stronger prospects for India. Three broad themes were a focus: geopolitical risks to remain elevated for the foreseeable future; inflation risks are becoming an increasingly important concern - energy prices and implications of AI; and potential risks from a severe El Niño. Press conference: choose your adventure We expect Chair Warsh’s Oct press conference to follow a similar template to Sep: only about 30 mins, with no follow-up questions. We have long been of the view that if he doesn’t want to make substantive remarks about the outlook, he is better served by saying less. This reduces the risk of unforced errors. Scenario 1: a hike In terms of content, we think Warsh will have an easier time at the presser if the Fed hikes than if it doesn’t. If the Fed hikes, he will probably emphasize that inflation continues to be too high and broad based, financial conditions aren’t sufficiently restrictive, economic activity is robust and the labor market is stable. The key challenge for Warsh in this scenario would be to not sound too hawkish. The hike alone would most likely cause significant tightening in financial conditions. His goal would be to ensure the move isn’t overdone, while still talking tough on inflation. This would be an easier needle to thread if Warsh were willing to give forward guidance. For example, he could use the term “midcycle adjustment” to signal to markets that the Fed probably won’t hike by more than 75-100bp in total. Japan Economic Flash: BOJ October Preview: We Expect Status Quo at the BOJ October Meeting 23 October 2026 | 3:07PM JST The Bank of Japan (BOJ) will hold its monetary policy meeting on October 29-30. n We think the BOJ has no need to conduct consecutive rate hikes, and we maintain our expectation that it will keep the policy rate at 1.25%. We expect no substantial changes to the economic and price assessments in the n BOJ’s October Outlook Report versus the previous July assessment. However, we see the board members’ core CPI forecast being adjusted downward for FY2026 accounting for the current low inflation rate, and upward for FY2027 on re-surging crude oil price. While the Composite Index of Inflation Expectations, which the BOJ focuses on n as a gauge of underlying inflation, is expected to have turned downward slightly in July-September quarter, we expect the BOJ’s language regarding upside risk to underlying inflation exceeding 2%, to be maintained exactly as in the July report. At the post meeting press conference, we will focus on the following points to n gauge insights on future rate hikes: (1) the Governor’s view on the current exchange rate and the upside risk to underlying inflation from yen depreciation, (2) the impact of tighter financial conditions driven by rate hikes, (3) the Bank’s current asses

Financial System Report also indicates that firms and households have become more resilient to higher interest rates In this regard, the BoJ’s October 2026 Financial System Report, released on 23 October, presented an analysis of the impact of higher interest rates on firms and households. Areas warranting attention include the wide variation in financial conditions among firms with net debt and, for households, rising loan sizes driven primarily by higher property prices, alongside an increase in ultra-long-term mortgages with maturities exceeding 35 years. Nevertheless, the report finds that corporate resilience to higher interest rates has improved overall: effectively debt-free firms have increased as a trend, while interest coverage ratios (ICRs) and debt ratios have shown gradual improvement even among firms with net debt. For households, the report concludes that improving employment and income conditions are helping ease repayment burdens, despite rising rates on variable-rate mortgages, which account for most housing loans. The BoJ therefore does not appear to view rate hikes as likely to become a major burden on firms and households in the near term. We continue to expect the next rate hike in December and a terminal rate of 2% We stick to our base case for rate hikes in December and in March and July 2027, taking the policy rate to a terminal level of 2%. Protests started in response to a new carbon tax for fuel and broadened out to include cost-of-living demands. These protests were most acute during late 2018 and fad- ed after the government scrapped the tax proposal and enacted measures to support purchasing power. INSEE estimates that the protests dragged the 4Q18 GDP print by 0.4%-pt ar, which was then followed by some payback. The Ministry of Finance last year also investigated the impact of protests, looking at the seven key episodes reported in Table 1. The analysis concluded that these protests on average dragged activity by 0.4% ar, followed by some payback after the protests ended (Figure 4). Elsewhere, tax refunds have likely been used and interest rates have moved higher as the Fed seeks faster convergence of inflation to the target. Finally, cuts to entitlement spending inside the OBBBA become a larger drag on the economy over time. If the OBBBA is implemented as written, then cuts to SNAP and Medicaid make fiscal policy a slight drag on consumption next year. Absent a much larger decline in equities that cause negative wealth effects to kick in, we expect affordability and fiscal pressures to weigh more heavily on spending growth for low- and middle-income consumers. Just how much spending growth slows remains an open question. We expect real consumption to grow 1.9% q/q saar in 4Q and 1.5% in 1Q, with most of the slowdown coming from goods. While strong durable goods purchases indicate to us that consumers feel confident enough to spend, durables also tend to be more volatile. As our autos equity research colleagues recently wrote, their companies have recently started to note a more price-sensitive consumer and affordability challenges potentially weighing on future sales. If we are correct and consumption growth moderates, then the Fed can continue to recalibrate policy to push against second-round effects of higher oil prices. If not, a more aggressive hiking cycle may still be needed.

M Idea 10 inflation. More broadly, the economy continues to operate with considerable excess supply. The labor market has cooled, trade uncertainty remains elevated, and wage pressures appear contained. These conditions should limit firms' ability to fully pass higher input costs on to consumers, restraining the overall acceleration in core inflation. However, domestic slack is now competing against a greater number of persistent external cost pressures. We expect it to limit the extent of the inflation pickup rather than fully offset it. From Non-Core to Core: Pass-Through Picks Up The most important change in our inflation outlook is the expected persistence of upstream cost pressures and their transmission into underlying inflation. We expect the direct energy shock to remain the dominant contributor to headline CPI through late 2026, but pass-through into core goods and services should begin to increase from 4Q26 and accelerate in 1Q27. We expect core inflation to move closer to 2.4%, above the levels suggested by the latest annual CPI-Median and CPI-Trim readings. This would represent a moderate acceleration rather than a broad inflation breakout. Domestic slack should continue to restrain housing and labor-intensive services inflation, while much of the increase remains concentrated in externally exposed goods, transportation- sensitive services and intermediate-input costs. In Chile, core services are running above 4%, the oil shock will add further pressures from volatiles if persistent, and El Niño introduces risks stemming from food prices. However, economic activity has been weak and that likely needs to improve for the BCCh to shift to a more hawkish communication. We expect year-end inflation at 4.3%. Core services inflation remains high, at 4.3%. For reference, core services averaged 3.7% in 2016-19, when headline averaged 3.0%. Empirical estimates suggest that stronger El Niño episodes are associated with an increase in headline inflation, particularly through climate-sensitive food categories such as fruits and vegetables. Sequential shocks to headline are likely to keep core services high as wage contracts incorporate past inflation. records.text: icing model based on market fundamentals suggests $94. How does this discrepancy arise? In this episode, we go through the basics of crude oil prices, as well as discuss the effects created by geography and risk premia. Oil Markets Weekly: Risk premium, geography discount What is the price of oil? Eight months into the war with Iran, what should be a straightforward question has become surprisingly hard to answer. Oil is once again flowing from the Middle East, and our pricing model puts Brent’s fair value at $94/bbl. Yet Brent is trading near $114, almost $20 above what fundamentals imply. Is this simply the price of geopolitical risk, or is something else influencing the value of oil? Of course, a model built solely on oil market fundamentals cannot capture every movement in prices. Uncertainty can push prices away from fair value, sometimes by a wide margin. During the COVID pandemic, crude traded at a discount of nearly $20/bbl to our model’s estimated value. In the first months following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, prices carried a premium of roughly $15. Deviations of this magnitude make forecasting oil prices considerably more difficult, even when the underlying supply and demand outlook is relatively clear. But before we attribute today’s nearly $20 gap entirely to geopolitics, we need to ask whether something else has changed in the way oil is being priced. The BoJ cannot attribute more aggressive hikes to external pressure At the US-Japan summit in September, concerns about JPY weakness were shared, and it became clear that the US Treasury continued to favor further rate hikes to address it (Reuters, 16 October). Since the BoJ cannot explain its monetary policy decisions as a response to external pressure, we think it will move to demonstrate accountability for future rate hikes by retaining a firm CPI outlook and emphasizing upside risks. Indeed, seemingly in response to the US Treasury’s comments, Governor Ueda has stepped up his hawkish rhetoric, saying that “we cannot tolerate any further upside deviation in underlying inflation” (Nikkei, 19 October). Consumption and capex have softened since the July Outlook Report Outlining economic and inflation developments since the July Outlook Report, economic activity has remained resilient overall, although the data present a mixed picture. Starting with the negatives, although GDP posted a respectable 1.4% q/q saar increase in April-June, consumption, a key component of domestic demand, was flat, while capex fell 3.6% for a second consecutive quarterly decline. Since wages and corporate earnings have been stronger than expected, we are not particularly concerned. Nevertheless, consumption and capex are likely in a temporary lull, warranting some caution. Q3-26 survey data for euro area has improved throughout the period, with the Q3 average of the closely watched PMI consistent with GDP growth of approximately 0.3% q/q. However, the discrepancy between the signals from hard data and soft (survey) data is particularly pronounced, creating considerable uncertainty surrounding the Q3 GDP outcome. The volatility of Irish GDP introduces a further complication. Against this backdrop, our overall nowcast points to growth of around 0.15% q/q. Once the uncertainty surrounding the Irish figures is factored in, the risks appear tilted towards 0.1% rather than 0.2%. records.text: ion in financial conditions Despite the rate hikes to date, financial conditions remain accommodative. The Tankan’s financial position DI continues to show a net balance of firms reporting easy conditions, including small firms (Figure 6). According to our analysis, the main determinants of the financial position DI are interest rates and business conditions, with the latter exerting the stronger influence. Even if the policy rate rises to 2% by next summer, as we expect, the net balance appears likely to remain on the easy side unless business conditions deteriorate sharply and substantially. Lending growth, which BoJ officials frequently cite, is also strong (Figure 7). If underlying inflation has broadly reached 2%, the need to maintain accommodative financial conditions diminishes. Moreover, if the BoJ is concerned about upside inflation risks, it makes sense to move financial conditions toward neutral through continued, timely rate hikes. Governor Ueda’s statement at the September meeting that “the phase of monetary policy has changed” is consistent with this. 23 October 2026 42 Barclays | Global Economics Weekly: When AI angst meets oil trouble

In addition to guarding against upside risks to underlying inflation, it is likely to difficult for the BoJ to ignore pressure from a US administration concerned about JPY weakness. We therefore think it is likely to be compelled to continue raising rates every three to four months for now, faster than the previous pace of roughly once every six months. The markets have fully priced in three US rate hikes by next summer. The BoJ also needs to monitor US rate hikes closely. Our CPI outlook and anticipated changes to the BoJ Board are the main reasons we expect rate hikes to end next July That said, we expect core-core CPI inflation, after rising to around 2.6% by next spring, to then ease and stabilize at around 2% from the autumn. We therefore think it will gradually become more difficult to justify further rate hikes thereafter. In addition, the terms of hawkish Board Members Takata and Tamura expire next July, and the Takaichi administration may nominate dovish successors, as it has to date. We consequently expect the BoJ to develop a stronger bias toward holding rates steady thereafter. These are the main reasons we expect the hiking cycle to end next July. However, if JPY weakness persists, or if the US administration effectively attempts to intervene even in BoJ nominations, the BoJ could be compelled to raise rates further. Institutional investors maintain an overweight position in European Industrials but there is room for those positions to increase (Figure 2). • Information Technology: Just a few companies reported this week but it generated a lot of headlines and continued the debate on the future of AI. Next week we will hear from the majority of large cap Tech, but so far results are mixed and markets are making a definite distinction between spenders and beneficiaries. Even though top line numbers mostly beat expectations, analysts are looking at the details of already high expectations (Figure 3). Major companies were penalized for spending too much and too little capex. Meanwhile, companies on the demand side of AI, reported strong results, making it clear that the orderbook is growing. • Consumer: Overall, there is a big divergence between the two consumer sectors. Staples has delivered overall positive earnings as companies see volume but not price recovery. Consumer demand is there but companies cannot pass the higher costs to consumers. The picture in Discretionary is bleaker with most companies disappointing so far (Figure 4). Airlines are feeling the impact of higher energy prices, Autos guide lower on weak sales and there is no demand for luxury coming from China or the US. records.text: Japan Rates Weekly 23 October 2026 Citi Research 4 fiscal year at around ¥27trn. Normally, it would be sufficient to make adjustments to 3m and 6m, but issuance of even 1y, which is made up exclusively by TBs, has fallen to ¥2.2trn each time. This is evidence of an excess of funds in the government sector. On the side of JGB issuance, sales to retail investors are exceeding the budgeted amount by more than ¥5trn on an annualized basis. Tax revenue is also strong, with progress toward the budgeted annual figure larger in April-August than it was last fiscal year. In total, the amount of excess easily exceeds ¥10trn. At end-September government deposits with the BoJ and outstanding reverse repo transactions with the government totaled some ¥33trn. This more than ¥15trn larger than a year earlier. Internal purchases within the exchequer were around the same in April-June as last fiscal year. After Brazil’s runoff, the next major political test for the framework discussed in this note will be Argentina’s 2027 presidential election. The October 2025 midterms gave Milei a renewed mandate and strengthened his position in Con- gress, creating greater scope to advance structural reforms. Yet the election did not eliminate the political constraints on implementation. LLA and its allies remain short of indepen- dent majorities, making continued negotiations essential, par- ticularly with provincial leaders, whose influence has increased as the political system has become more fragment- ed. The 2027 presidential election will therefore present a differ- ent test from the anti-incumbency contests that characterized much of 2025-26. Rather than asking whether voters are will- ing to change course, the question will be whether they remain willing to stay the course. By then, stabilization may have substantially reduced macroeconomic distortions with- out yet delivering its full economic dividend. Investment is likely to respond before consumption, and many of the gains from structural reforms may still be at an early stage. records.text: o the MMF complex. Below, we examine several aspects of the macro environment that have likely contributed to slower inflows. Chief among them is the compression of MMF yields relative to bank deposit rates. At the same time, the location of leverage creation within the financial system appears to be shifting. Hedge fund borrowing associated with Treasury basis and relative-value trades has moderated, while traditional bank lending channels have expanded. To the extent balance sheet expansion is increasingly being facilitated through the banking system rather than the non-bank financial sector, the resulting cash creation is more likely to remain in bank deposits rather than flow into MMFs. But overall cash is growing at a healthy clip, and the allocation mix between deposits and MMFs depends heavily on relative yields. We think that means the Fed rate hikes our economists expect should help tilt the balance of flows back toward money funds. The yield advantage of MMFs over bank deposits has narrowed significantly. After the Fed cut rates by 175bp from peak to trough, the yield spread between money funds and bank deposits fell to roughly 130bp as of Q2. The reduced incentive to move cash out of deposits has translated into less deposit flight into MMFs compared with the past several years. Nor did the ECB respond with a dedicated anti-spread tool during earlier episodes when Italian spreads moved above 300bp amid political stress. Ahead of the French presidential election, the hurdle for intervention may be even higher. Neither of the leading candidates is campaigning on meaningful fiscal consolidation, making it difficult for the ECB to justify stepping in to suppress spreads before the political direction becomes clearer.
