records.text: ab 23 October 2026 Global Research Japan Macro Watch BoJ's hiking cycle has further to run BoJ still has work to do even after underlying inflation reaches 2% We expect the BoJ to keep the policy rate unchanged at 1.25% at its October meeting, although hawkish board member Takata may dissent in favor of further tightening. The Outlook Report should show only limited revisions, with growth forecasts largely unchanged and inflation projections slightly higher. The key issue is whether the BoJ formally recognizes underlying inflation as having reached around 2%. While such an assessment would be consistent with Governor Ueda’s recent comments, it would not imply the end of the hiking cycle. Inflation risks remain skewed to the upside, financial conditions are still accommodative, and policymakers continue to emphasize the need to stabilize inflation sustainably around 2%. Recent data, including the Tankan survey and CPI figures, support additional tightening. Combined with hawkish policy signals, we expect the BoJ to raise rates again in December and gradually move the policy rate toward 2%. Financial conditions are a key guide for further BoJ tightening The BoJ continues to raise rates on the view that financial conditions remain accommodative and is likely to maintain its hiking cycle as long as this assessment holds, in our view. Is there an upper bound to the basis widening in a sell-off? Despite the directionality of the underlying clearing imbalances to rates, there should be an economic limit to how much the swap rates on identical swaps can differ between two venues. While there are several frictions that lead to the emergence of clearinghouse basis, such as capital and operational charges, the principal cost is having to post additional initial margin. But the margin cost is by itself not linked to the level of rates because initial margins are a function of interest rate risk, not of the level of rates. Because of this, if basis between two clearinghouses gets sufficiently wide, it should fully offset the cost of at least some participants who are able to clear at both venues to arbitrage between the two. Once such a point is reached, there is limit to how much the basis can further widen regardless of how much rates sell off. It is difficult to accurately pinpoint this economic bound. Conceptually, it depends on: 1) the initial margin required, which is a function of the tenor of swaps; 2) the difference between the cost of funding the margin and the interest rate earned on it, which is a proxy for unsecured vs secured funding spreads; and 3) the amount of time the position will need to be maintained before the basis converges (accounting for the fac

records.text: The trajectory of retail and household equity demand Rotations in the equity market this week reflected a sharp hedge fund derisking. On Thursday our Hedge Fund VIP long/short basket pair fell by 4%, a decline only rivaled during the past decade on DeepSeek Monday in January 2025 and during the COVID sell-off in March 2020. Likewise, GS Prime Services data show a large decline in gross leverage that has contributed to an unusually challenging environment for hedge fund returns. Following the unwind of the last two weeks, they estimate that fundamental hedge fund net leverage registers close to 5-year lows while gross leverage remains well above historical averages. While hedge funds cut risk, the past few weeks have shown an uptick in engagement among retail traders, who otherwise have pulled back from the equity market in recent months. GS Global Banking & Markets estimates show a modest increase in retail trading activity during the past two weeks, but retail volumes have declined by about 20% since mid-summer and more than 40% since late 2025. As we discussed in China AI Watch: More growth, less reflation(open in new tab), China’s scale and supply-chain advantages position it to capture an outsized share of the global AI hardware cycle, with AI exports estimated to add 0.5pp to GDP growth in 2026. China is increasingly a manufacturing hub for the global AI buildout, spanning servers, semiconductors, AI-enabled electronics, cooling systems and batteries. AI-related products now account for 23% of total exports and more than half of China’s export growth in 2026 YTD. The divergence between resilient production and weak (domestic) demand remains striking. In contrast to the 4.5% GDP growth print and average IP growth of 5.1% in Q3, we estimate that the weighted average of key demand indicators, including retail sales, FAI and exports, deflated by core CPI, grew by just 0.6% y/y. In our view, the large gap between GDP growth and demand indicators reflects two factors: 1) China’s GDP is measured from the production side; and 2) industrial and services production has remained considerably more resilient than underlying domestic demand. We think the prolonged weakness in domestic demand reflects some structural factors. Consumption remains constrained by household deleveraging, property-driven wealth erosion, and a weak labour market. We expect retail sales growth to slow to around 1% this year from 3.7% in 2025. ECB: Following the framework, hiking in December We expect the ECB to leave the policy rates unchanged at its 29 October meeting, keeping the deposit rate at 2.50%, the upper bound of estimates of the nominal neutral rate. While realised growth and inflation have broadly aligned with ECB expectations since the September meeting, the deterioration in the energy outlook has strengthened the case for further tightening. The decision to hold rates predominantely reflects the ECB's assessment that the current shock still falls within the middle-case scenario outlined in the 2025 strategy review, which warrants a measured and gradual response – a point that has been repeatedly reemphasized by members of the GC. More broadly, the ECB is likely to have assessed that the economy has shown encouraging resilience over the past few months. The combination of supportive fiscal policy and strong demand due to the global AI cycle has supported activity. That being said, higher energy prices and tighter financial conditions tilt the balance of risks to the downside. Indeed, incoming hard data paint a mixed picture of Q3 activity, with retail sales and industrial production pointing to subdued activity. On communication, we do not expect a material shift. Fundamentally, fiscal risk continues to cap any durable yen bid, and markets cannot be faulted for being skeptical of official assurances of fiscal prudence. The FY27 budget and bond issuance plan, due by end-December, should bring this into sharper focus; media reports already point to fresh energy/gas subsidies and dining-out support tied to the con- sumption tax cut, with no clear funding source beyond the administration leaning further on bond issuance. The October BoJ meeting is unlikely to be the catalyst that breaks this range, even as the Bank formally claims a historic milestone. Per Reuters, the BoJ is set to acknowl- edge in its Outlook Report that it has hit the 2% inflation tar- get for the first time in nearly 14 years — but we expect this to validate the September hike and underpin a quarterly tight- ening cadence rather than spur back-to-back moves, as the BoJ will want time to assess policy transmission before acting again. Because a quarterly pace of rate hikes is already priced into the OIS curve, confirmation alone is unlikely to lift ter- minal pricing, and the Bank's reluctance to signal consecutive hikes could cap more aggressive tightening bets — leaving limited scope for material JPY appreciation out of the Octo- ber MPM, and leaves the currency more exposed to global risk and rates developments. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 • The balance of inflation risks is now clearly skewed to the upside, although excess supply limits the case for further tightening. Shelter remains the principal domestic disinflationary offset. Higher energy prices also support Canadian national income and some activity through the terms of trade, but the investment response is likely smaller than in previous cycles. We expect the second hike in January, allowing the Bank to assess additional inflation data before completing its policy adjustment. Bank of Canada Implications We now expect the Bank of Canada to raise its policy rate by 25bp in October and again in January, taking the terminal rate to 2.75%. This replaces our forecast for rates to remain at 2.25% through 2027. Our assessment of the September meeting emphasized that upside inflation risks had increased but that contained core inflation, excess supply, and trade uncertainty still argued against tightening. Inflation risks had risen even though realized pass-through remained limited. What has changed is our assessment of the persistence of the energy shock, its implications for firms' pricing decisions, and communications from policymakers over the past week. Taken together, these developments now argue for a modest upward recalibration of policy rather than an extended hold. Since wages and corporate earnings have been stronger than expected, we are not particularly concerned. Nevertheless, consumption and capex are likely in a temporary lull, warranting some caution. Turning to the positives, wages come first. Through August, scheduled cash earnings maintained y/y growth of 3% or more for eight consecutive months. By this time of year, the reflection of shunto base-pay increases into scheduled cash earnings is normally largely complete. Based on the historical relationship between base-pay increases and scheduled cash earnings, we estimate FY26 growth in scheduled cash earnings at 2.5%, but actual earnings have continued to grow faster than that. Second, the September Tankan showed an improvement in the manufacturing business conditions DI for both large and small firms, led by global AI-related demand, while the non-manufacturing DI remained elevated ( Figure 2). Relative to our forecast, core-core CPI surprised on the upside by 0.2ppt. Energy inflation was broadly unchanged, moving only slightly from -0.7% to -0.6%, while services inflation and core goods inflation (goods excluding food and energy) accounted for nearly all of the acceleration, each contributing roughly half. Services inflation remained broad-based, though accommodation prices stood out as particularly strong. Among core goods, tissue paper prices rose 18% y/y, partly reflecting higher oil prices. Consumer electronics were even stronger, with video recorders up 38% and tablets up 29%. Rising memory prices linked to AI-related demand are also becoming increasingly evident. Among approximately 600 CPI items, memory cards posted the fastest price increase, surging 152%y/y. Food inflation edged up from 2.7% to 2.9%, but lower rice prices suggest that a sustained reacceleration has not yet taken hold. Incorporating the latest data, we have revised our inflation forecasts modestly higher. We expect core CPI to accelerate from 2.1% in September to 3.0% by December, aided by energy-related effects. Inflation is likely to peak at around 3.9% in February next year due to base effects associated with energy subsidies. Moreover, if the BoJ is concerned about upside inflation risks, it makes sense to move financial conditions toward neutral through continued, timely rate hikes. Governor Ueda’s statement at the September meeting that “the phase of monetary policy has changed” is consistent with this. In this regard, the BoJ’s October 2026 Financial System Report, released on 23 October, presented an analysis of the impact of higher interest rates on firms and households. Areas warranting attention include the wide variation in financial conditions among firms with net debt and, for households, rising loan sizes driven primarily by higher property prices, alongside an increase in ultra-long-term mortgages with maturities exceeding 35 years. Nevertheless, the report finds that corporate resilience to higher interest rates has improved overall: effectively debt-free firms have increased as a trend, while interest coverage ratios (ICRs) and debt ratios have shown gradual improvement even among firms with net debt. For households, the report concludes that improving employment and income conditions are helping ease repayment burdens, despite rising rates on variable-rate mortgages, which account for most housing loans. A more persistent energy shock, growing risks of pass- through into core inflation, and recent BoC communications have shifted the policy outlook. We see this as a measured 50bp recalibration to a more persistent inflation outlook, rather than the beginning of a sustained tightening cycle. After faster appreciation around the Trump-Xi summit n in September, the Chinese Renminbi has reverted to a steadier appreciation pace in recent weeks, and is now approaching our 3m USD/CNY target of 6.70, with the offshore spot having broken decisively stronger than that. Notwithstanding all the global macro volatility, the basic story here is unchanged. A combination of weak domestic demand, strong competitiveness and an undervalued currency means that net exports continue to make an outsized contribution to China’s GDP growth, and the current account surplus is on its way to a historically unprecedented level as a share of global GDP (Exhibit 4). The latest forecast updates in the IMF’s WEO take another step in that direction, but we still think that they underestimate the scope for Chinese exports to increase further. In the latest data, the trade surplus expanded to US$133.5bn (NSA) in September, the largest monthly surplus on record. Likewise, we continue to think that a gradual but sustained currency appreciation is underway but consensus forecasts and forward markets underestimate how far this process can run given the deep undervaluation starting point. Ultimately, currency appreciation alone will not address China’s economic challenges—as we have argued previously, that needs both currency appreciation and support for domestic demand, two instruments to hit two targets. records.text: M Idea 6 Oil Tracker: Running out of buffers Our baseline outlook for the U.S. economy assumes a permanent oil risk premium. The renewed pressure on energy prices has dragged the world into the seventh month of this prolonged energy price shock. Historically, episodes of acute geopolitical or physical supply disruption have mostly lasted 3–6 months, with the notable exception of the 1978–79 oil shock and its aftermath. As buffers such as higher U.S. exports, weaker Chinese imports, and ample inventories begin to fade, we update our oil tracker to highlight developments and trends that matter for U.S. economic growth. The latest data suggest that crude oil inventories in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) are barely declining after reaching historic lows, but commercial stocks are falling faster than they were as production declined in the last couple of weeks. U.S. crude oil imports and exports both remain on an upward trend. Crude oil prices have continued to rise, while diesel margins have widened further. However, secondary-market equity purchases do not necessarily drain cash from MMFs. For every buyer there is a seller. While ownership of the cash changes, the cash itself more likely than not remains invested in money funds, rather than migrating into deposits. As a result, elevated equity trading volumes alone should not have a significant effect on aggregate MMF flows. Primary issuance is different. Equity issuance has been robust this year, and Federal Reserve data through Q2 show a meaningful pickup in net issuance by non-financial corporates (Figure 6). On an annualized basis, net issuance in Q2 was roughly $900bn higher than during the same period a year earlier. More broadly, net issuance has turned positive after several years in which buybacks reduced the amount of equity outstanding. records.text: h) is being met directly by running down FX reserves. Further, the sharp decline in banking liquidity surplus has also resulted in a tightening in monetary conditions. There- fore, tighter liquidity is inducing the market to do some of the RBI’s work. Markets have priced in a full 50 bps hike at the December review on the back of crude prices rising and the Governor's recent comments where he noted: “We normally do not use monetary policy to address financial stability risks. We follow the separation principle – monetary policy for price stability and targeted regulatory, supervisory and macroprudential tools for financial stability reasons, but they cannot be separated completely. It is important to keep in mind that monetary policy can have a bearing on financial stability. Therefore, monetary policy has to keep financial sta- bility in mind while taking decisions and can also be used for this purpose.” While the odds of a larger hike have increased, we maintain our call for a 25 bps hike for now because (i) the Rupee appears to have stabilized; (ii) core momentum softened in September; (iii) the MPC minutes continue to suggest data- dependence; and (iv) tighter liquidity conditions are doing some of the RBI’s work for it. But if crude increases further, underlying inflation broadens more and/or the Rupee comes under renewed pressure, the odds of a larger hike in December and a longer hiking cycle will increase materially. Export-led industrial strength continues to mask weak domestic demand. With the growth target largely secured, we see a higher bar for large-scale stimulus. Q3 GDP uptick puts 2026 growth target within reach China’s Q3 GDP growth beat expectations, edging up to 4.5% y/y from 4.3% in Q2 (consensus: 4.4%; Barclays: 4.3%). YTD growth now stands at 4.6% y/y, putting the 4.5-5% full-year target within reach. Even if growth slows to 4.2% in Q4, China would still reach the lower bound of the target range. September activity data also showed a modest improvement in domestic demand, but activity remains very subdued by historical standards: retail sales growth rose to 1.1% y/y, while the contraction in FAI narrowed slightly to -7.2% y/y YTD, supported by infrastructure and manufacturing investment. Reflecting the better-than-expected Q3 GDP print, we nudge up our 2026 growth forecast to 4.6% from 4.5%, but maintain our 2027 forecast of 4.0%. We think the modest improvement in GDP growth was largely driven by stronger industrial production, underpinned by continued export outperformance, particularly in AI-related and green-tech products. As discussed later, given that a rapid rise in long-term inflation expectations, as seen in the US in 2022, cannot be confirmed in Japan at present, we think the BOJ has no need to conduct consecutive rate hikes and we maintain our expectation that it will keep the policy rate at 1.25% at its MPM on October 29-30. The increase is likely to be driven by energy, food and sea- sonal clothing prices. Our nowcasting model tracks signifi- cant increases in fresh fruit and vegetable prices after two months of favorable prints. Meanwhile, elevated Brent prices continue to push energy prices higher, and the arrival of win- ter clothing adds further to the monthly print. Underlying inflation, by contrast, looks benign, as slowing economic activity limits price pressures in services and core goods (Fig- ure 3). Food prices are set to rise 3.1% m/m, led by a sharp 10% m/ m increase in fresh fruit and vegetable prices. With elevated Brent oil prices at $110 per barrel, we are tracking a 4.2% m/ m rise in energy prices, which also continues to exert upwards pressure to our end-26 forecast. Meanwhile, clothing prices are expected to rise 12.3% m/m due to the introduction of winter clothing. Core inflation, however, remains subdued. We expect services inflation of 1.5% m/m, with rents as the main contributor at 2.3% m/m, although rent inflation is grad- ually losing momentum. 23 October 2026 Focus Europe Deutsche Bank AG Page 7 Our sense is the hurdle to changing the QT plans is high, especially when there is an inflation threat. Slowing or stopped QT eases the monetary policy stance. The easiest way to do this would be for the ECB to hike less than priced – in the ECB’s policy tool hierarchy, policy rates have primacy. This is in effect what the ECB said in the September Accounts and what President Lagarde said to the European Parliament on 28 September: higher global yields can crowd out the need to tighten policy rates. Given that policy rates are 2.50% and the market is pricing three further hikes to 3.25%, there is room for the market to price out rate hikes before QT becomes relevant. In short, the rise in global yields is less a problem and more part of the solution, given the inflation threat. Financial conditions were starting to tighten quickly in September, but the pressures have peaked. According to the ECB’s MF -FCI, the peak tightening of financial conditions was on 29 September, before the big spike in OAT yields. After Lagarde’s comments at the European Parliament, the market priced out an ECB hike and capped the tightening in financial conditions despite the increase in French risk premia. This tells us two things. First, the ECB is happy to use higher yields/tighter financial conditions to lean against inflation. Second, the situation would need to change markedly for the ECB to think about slowing or stopping QT. Figure 11: The

centrated in externally exposed goods, transportation- sensitive services and intermediate-input costs. The broader risk is that several individually manageable shocks arrive simultaneously. Higher energy, food, semiconductor, and freight costs can each be partially absorbed through margins, inventories, and contracts. However, their combined effect is more difficult to offset, particularly after firms have already absorbed higher tariff and supply-chain costs over the past year. The balance of inflation risks is therefore clearly skewed to the upside. A faster normalization of energy prices or weaker domestic demand could limit pass- through, but persistent energy inflation, renewed food-price pressures, rising imported goods costs, and greater willingness among firms to pass through costs all increase the risk that underlying inflation remains above target. This is the basis for our revised policy call. The latest CPI release does not establish that generalized inflation has returned, but monetary policy must respond to the inflation outlook rather than the latest annual readings alone. We now expect the BoC to deliver two 25bp insurance hikes, in October and January, taking the policy rate to 2.75%. Considerable domestic slack should prevent the need for further tightening, but the persistence of the supply shock and the resulting rise in our core inflation forecasts make an extended hold increasingly difficult to justify.

records.text: M Idea 6 Tracking vegetable prices from weekly wholesale data Weekly wholesale prices can inform monthly HICP prices for vegetables and fruits: Prices for vegetables and fruits tend to be volatile, with swings that often exceed usual seasonality (eg due to particular weather conditions in a given month). However, to inform the near-term forecast we can resort to price signals from wholesale prices. Specifically, we use weekly wholesale prices from major markets in Germany and France to track near-term developments in consumer fruit and vegetable prices (see here and here). The data are available at a granular product level and at a weekly frequency1. We construct a wholesale price proxy for Germany and France: Equipped with the weekly product-level prices we sort items into the 5-digit level HICP subindices (using equal weights within the subindex) and aggregate to the 4-digit level (ie 'Vegetables/Tubers/Plantains/Cooking Bananas/Pulses' referred to as 'vegetables' and 'Fruits and Nuts' for 'fruits') using the respective HICP weights. Exhibit 16to Exhibit 19show the month-on-month growth rates of our wholesale price proxies against the respective HICP series. Consumer prices in both countries tend to move closely with wholesale prices (contemporaneous correlation between 0.5-0.7 across the four pairs during 2025-26), with higher volatility in wholesale prices in Germany. Unlike a freely traded spot price, an OSP is set by the producer and reflects a blend of market conditions, competing crude grades, refinery economics, and commercial strategy. A reduction in the OSP differential may signal weakening demand, but it could just as easily represent an attempt to protect market share or compensate buyers for higher transportation costs. We began to see this dynamic in early July 2026. After the US signed the MoU with Iran, more Hormuz-linked barrels flowed back into the market, but buying remained cautious. Producers therefore had to compete more aggressively for market share in Asia. Saudi Arabia’s July 6 announcement underscored that shift. It set some of the deepest discounts for August deliveries to Asian buyers—levels comparable only to the COVID period—and the month-on-month cut was described as the steepest in roughly two decades. By October, those discounts had widened further, moving from roughly $3 to $7 versus Dubai for November delivery across different grades—a $14/bbl swing in the differential in just four months (Figure 1). records.text: s The first risk-off cocktail ingredient remains the Iran war and geopolitical tensions in the Middle East. On the one hand, prospects for reportedly increased military operations following the US midterm elections are keeping crude prices above $110/bbl. On the other hand, rising hostilities increasingly hitting refining capacity continue to take a toll on refined products including diesel (Exhibit 1). The situation remains fluid and remarkably uncertain, but it remains difficult to see a trigger for de-escalation in the near future. The energy price factor is likely to keep putting pressure on inflation, or at the very least not provide material relief into next year. Sustained disinflation may need to be found somewhere else in the basket. Underneath the surface, AI concerns go beyond debt issuance The US equity market is selling off primarily driven by a correction in AI stocks (Exhibit 2). The common narrative is that the market is increasingly concerned about companies’ rising needs for further debt issuance to finance the AI investment boom. But something in this narrative doesn’t add up. records.text: improves. Those views remain conditional on energy relief materialising, however. With further natural gas relief dependent on greater clarity over winter weather, delayed inflation relief could leave both nominal longs and inflation shorts facing near-term headwinds, potentially offering better entry points further down the line. Beyond this, we also see scope for steeper inflation curves in the Euro area and the UK (Exhibit 9). If energy pressures ease, the near-term inflation premium could unwind, pulling front-end pricing lower. Alternatively, if the inflation shock proves more persistent, markets could reassess how quickly its inflationary effects will fade, extending the repricing further out the curve. Inflation curve steepeners could therefore benefit either from near-term inflation relief or from a reassessment of the length of the energy price shock (Exhibit 9). Overall, our baseline is that fading supply shocks will bring inflation relief across the G3 in 2027, but how that relief is priced will likely differ across markets. We think the case for real rate longs over nominals is clearer in the US compared to Europe where there is more value to a short inflation bias alongside steeper inflation curves in the Euro area and the UK. The key distinction is whether disinflation comes from easing supply shocks or weaker demand. In the case of the latter, nominal longs would offer clearer value relative to real rates. It is entirely plausible that this script repeats again, as it did after the initial Iran shock in March, which is why a core allocation to FX carry cannot be jettisoned. . However, two factors distinguish the current setup from Q1 in ways that have historically proven unfriendly to a benign FX resolu- tion. First, the rates backdrop has inverted: expectations of Fed cuts have given way to tightening expectations that put the dollar on a trend-appreciation path, removing the easing cushion that helped cap FX stress during the Iran shock. Sec- ond, the Euro's vulnerability has shifted from cyclical to structural: the French political/fiscal challenge is pushing ECB expectations in a more dovish direction even as spreads widen — a combination that, unlike the March European rates VaR shock, offers the EUR no offsetting yield cushion. Beyond these two mechanical shifts, the stakes are arguably higher in the current AI super-cycle than in the past, both as a generator of financial asset returns and as a key driver of the macro cycle via capex and wealth-effect/consumption chan- nels — reinforcing the case for vigilance against a more dura- ble crack in the AI narrative. records.text: Agency MBS Mortgage REITs avoid having to sell agency MBS despite September’s portfolio duration extension We had previously noted that, despite 10-year Treasury yields reaching as high as 5.3% in September, the MBS market is much healthier than in October 2023, when 10-year yields sold-off to touch then multi-decade highs of 5.0%. While there has been some deleveraging among levered holders of CMO floaters, forced selling of MBS has been very limited compared with 2023. Q3 earnings from mortgage REITs reporting earlier this week confirmed that REITs were indeed not sellers of agency MBS. Rather, most large mortgage REITs were net buyers of agency MBS on a face-value basis despite the sharp rate sell-off and duration extension their portfolios experienced in September (Exhibit 1). These purchases were supported by sizable equity raises during the quarter. Although REIT share prices declined in September, the declines were broadly in line with the erosion in book values, leaving P/B ratios at levels that remained accretive for equity issuance (Exhibit 2). In addition, mortgage REITs also entered the quarter with relatively conservative leverage. Leverage ticked up modestly during Q3 but remains slightly below its longer-term average (Exhibit 3). Finally, REIT portfolios were already relatively slow-prepaying, at roughly 8–10 CPR, leaving less room for incremental duration extension from a further slowdown in prepayments. The impact is highly country-specific. El Niño can transmit through several channels. Weaker agricultural output can push up food inflation - already seeing early evidence in recent months with Asia's downward revision of yield on oil palm, rice and maize, lower hydropower generation can raise dependence on alternative fuels such as LNG imports (already disrupted by the ongoing Middle East crisis), and government support or disaster-related spending can add to fiscal pressures. On a more sector level, Asia's semiconductors are also exposed to volatile water stress situations with ultra-low water reservoir levels seen in Taiwan and Korea. records.text: US Rates Weekly 23 October 2026 Citi Research 8 Relative value: Shorting the belly in 5s7s10s We fade the recent richening in the 7y point heading into the auction next week by shorting the belly in a weighted 5s7s10s fly. The recent risk-off move in markets has led to the rates curve bull flattening, led by the belly of the curve. The 7y point outperformed on the curve as the 5s7s10s fly moved lower by about 3bp since the start of this month. This does not surprise us as 7s have typically outperformed in recent risk-off driven rate rallies. In Figure 13, we show the changes in the 5s7s10s fly during risk-off episodes over the last year. We filtered for days in which equities (S&P 500) sold off by more than 1% and 10y rates rallied by more than 5bps. We had seven such days over the last year, including yesterday, and in each of those instances, we saw the 5s7s10s fly moving lower. One possible explanation for this move could be that non-rates investors typically buy the TY contract as a hedge during such risk-off moves. Note: Futures trading involves substantial risk of loss. Construction investment, which has been a notable source of resilience for the Italian economy since the post-pandemic reopening, is set to contribute negative to real GDP growth for the first time in two years as monthly production in construction tracks 3.4% below the Q2 level so far in Q3. Methodology: Estimating El Niño Pass-Through to Canadian Inflation We estimate the impact of a Very Strong El Niño on Canadian inflation through three separately estimated channels, combining global food-price responses, domestic pass-through, and local weather effects. 1. El Niño to global food prices. Following the ECB's Adolfsen–Lappé methodology, we estimate Jordà local projections of the FAO food-price index on the Oceanic Niño Index (ONI), controlling for fertilizer prices, oil prices, and world industrial production, with HAC-robust standard errors. The estimated response to a 1°C ONI increase is scaled to a Very Strong El Niño (+2.0°C in our central scenario and +2.5°C in the high scenario). Global food prices initially decline modestly before rising as weather disruptions affect harvests, inventories, and exportable supply. The estimated response reaches approximately 9% after twelve months and peaks near 12% after sixteen months. 2. Global food prices to Canadian CPI. We estimate a distributed-lag ARDL model linking monthly FAO food-price inflation to Canadian food and headline CPI inflation, controlling for contemporaneous Brent prices and three lags of domestic inflation. Food was the main source of the upside surprise relative to our expectations, increasing its contribution by 0.10pp, with more than half of food items recording price gains of at least 3% y/y as the effects of Middle East disruptions spread to consumers. Rice’s negative contribution widened, but by less than the 0.08pp we had expected. However, distribution of the new rice crop will gather pace from October, and rice's negative contribution is expected to widen further with potential impact on household inflation expectations as well. Japan Economics Focus September CPI: Back above 2% across the board Both core-core and core rose sharply to above 2% y/y, driven by travel, policy factors, household appliances/daily necessities and food. We expect core-core near 3.0% in spring as oil/JPY pass-thru strengthens, despite rice drag. It should then decline and stabilize around 2% in autumn 2027. • Nationwide CPI inflation excluding perishables and energy (core-core) rose sharply to +2.4% in September (August: +1.9%), reaching the 2% threshold for the first time in six months based on data released by MIC on 23 October. Seasonally adjusted, inflation accelerated to 0.5% m/m (0.3%), marking a third consecutive month at 0.3% or higher. • The CPI excluding perishables alone (core) strengthened to +2.1% (+1.7%), reaching the 2% level for the first time in nine months. Month on month, the index accelerated to +0.5% (+0.1%). Overall CPI inflation also rose at a faster pace, to +2.1% y/y (+1.9%). • The main drivers of the y/y rise in core-core CPI inflation were (1) travel-related prices, (2) water charges and childcare fees, (3) household appliances and daily necessities and (4) food excluding perishables and rice. • Food excluding perishables and rice was the main driver of the upside surprise relative to our forecast, increasing its contribution to y/y core-core inflation by 0.10pp. More than half of the items recorded y/y price increases

records.text: This has prompted two major shifts in recently issued non-qualified mortgage (non-QM) RMBS deal structures. Shift to a sequential cashflow waterfall protects the A-1 tranche and encourages deal callability, albeit at the expense of a longer weighted-average life (WAL) for the A-2 and A-3 tranches. Amongst recent non-QM RMBS deals, a notable structural change in principal repayment allocations has emerged across senior tranches (A-1, A-2, and A-3 tranches). Issuers have increasingly shifted from the traditional modified sequential repayment structure in favor of a purely sequential waterfall. Under the modified sequential framework, principal repayments were distributed pro-rata across the senior tranches, while mezzanine and subordinate tranches received payments sequentially only after the seniors were fully retired. However, heightened investor sensitivity to extension risk—driven by elevated benchmark rates and declining economic incentives for issuers to call deals—has prompted recent transactions to adopt a fully sequential framework. Under this structure, 100% of available principal is directed to the A-1 tranche until it is fully paid down, before any cash flows are allocated sequentially to the A-2 and A-3 tranches, followed by the mezzanine and subordinate tranches. By paying down the A-1 tranche first, A-1 tranche investors benefit with greater protection from extension risk. To be clear, our point is not to say there should be no efforts to structurally reduce the level of public spending and lower taxation. Both are higher than elsewhere. Nor do we think that the required amount of consolidation can be achieved only from higher taxes. And we also suspect tax hikes would likely be an unpopular political choice. But meaningful spending cuts are difficult to implement in the short term. The fastest path to a lower deficit, say closer to 4%, would therefore likely be through higher taxes. We note that the government is already moving in this direction, with tax increases since 2024 amounting to 1.1pp of GDP. While further tax increases would be unlikely to support growth in an already weak economy, there may be an offsetting effect to the extent that tighter fiscal policy strengthens confidence in the fiscal trajectory and, in turn, contributes to an easing in financial conditions (see here for our discussion of the impact of tighter financial conditions on the economy). In short, we think the government still has options to deliver a lower deficit than currently planned. Such measures could also help ease market concerns around the fiscal outlook. records.text: g of incumbency has coincided with an appar- ent decline in the electoral returns to fiscal support. Using a panel of 44 presidential elections in nine Latin American countries since 2004, we estimate rolling eight-year partial correlations between the incumbent side’s first-round vote share and different measures of the fiscal stance, controlling for economic growth, inflation, the incumbent bloc’s previous vote share, and whether the sitting president was on the bal- lot. The results point to a gradual shift. Real primary spending growth over the term was positively correlated with the incumbent vote in every window through the end of the last decade, but that relationship weakened thereafter and turned negative in the two most recent windows. Election-year struc- tural fiscal loosening shows a similar, but more pronounced reversal (Figure 2). The exercise should be interpreted cautiously: each window contains only 13 to 17 elections, adjacent windows share most of their observations and not all estimates are statistical- ly distinguishable from zero. Also, the effect of the pandemic on elections held between 2020 and 2022, in particular, could also bias the results. Even so, the broad direction is consistent across the fiscal measures. Fiscal expansion appears to have become progressively less effective as a source of electoral protection, reinforcing the view that the recent anti-incum- bency wave cannot be understood simply as a reaction to insufficient political support

records.text: Tighter excess spread drives interest diversion up the subordinate capital stack. Another notable structural evolution involves the expansion of interest diversion mechanics used to fund senior tranche coupon step-ups. When a non-QM RMBS deal is not called within the first 48 months, the coupon on the senior tranches steps up by 100bp. Traditionally, to pay this stepped-up coupon, the interest of the B-3 tranche can be used to supplement excess interest in the deal. Recent structures have expanded this mechanism up the capital stack by using interest from the B-2 and even B-1 tranches (in some cases) to supplement interest cashflows available for making the step-up coupon. In certain recent deals, the B-2 bonds (or even B-1 bonds) become Principal Only (PO) bonds and stop accruing any interest after 48 months. The primary catalyst for this shift has been the material compression in the spread “cushion” between the collateral gross weighted-average coupon (GWAC) and its respective cost of financing amidst rising rates over recent months. Across a sample of recent deals, we estimate this cushion exceeded 120 bps in July before tightening down to roughly 50–75 bps in early October. At current levels, interest on the B-3 alone may not be sufficient to fund the senior tranche step-up across a range of prepay and default scenarios, prompting the inclusion of additional subordinate tranches. records.text: wer long-end Treasury supply has also supported spreads; we expect the Treasury to keep auction sizes unchanged at the November refunding, but tweak guidance to preserve flexibility and timing • Despite these near-term supportive factors, fiscal deficits and the longer-run Treasury supply outlook remain a structural force arguing for tighter long-end spreads in the medium term. While spreads may be less vulnerable, they are not immune to larger shocks. Long-end swap spreads have been resilient in recent months and spread volatility has been benign (Figure 1 and Figure 2). While spreads widened alongside the rise in yields, they have not retraced even as long-end rates fell from decade highs. Notably, the sell-off in equities tied to worries about the AI ecosystem and growth concerns did little to pressure spreads lower. Increased balance sheet capacity, Treasury buybacks and benign funding conditions have moderated the moves in risk-off episodes. At the same time, corporate pre-hedging activity tied to AI financing needs has provided support as borrowers compete for capital. In the current environment, we believe the hurdle for long-end spreads to tighten has increased and the transmission mechanism appears weaker. However, fiscal deficits and elevated Treasury borrowing needs remain the dominant driver for spreads, and they are not immune to larger risk-off moves that could tighten spreads. records.text: Tokyo trading on the 23rd. CHF also attracted safe-haven demand, while JPY crosses fell across the board. We attribute the elevated level of USDJPY to the still-wide US-Japan interest rate differential, reduced safe-haven demand associated with a widening equity risk premium and fiscal concerns surrounding the Takaichi administration’s “high-pressure economy” policies. Among these, we see the equity risk premium as particularly influential. This week, the unwind of AI trades spread into broader market caution, while concerns about an economic slowdown intensified. A narrowing equity risk premium has consequently helped restore demand for the JPY as a safe haven. Although oil prices rose further amid heightened geopolitical risks, bond markets did not price in a more hawkish policy outlook. Instead, terminal-rate pricing declined, suggesting growing concern about an economic slowdown. Depending on risk sentiment and the extent of carry-trade unwinds, we believe there remains scope for some further JPY appreciation, although the 155 level should provide initial support. Both the FOMC on the 28th and the BoJ meeting on the 30th are widely expected to leave policy unchanged. Many Fed officials have indicated that there is no need to rush into further hikes following September’s increase. This includes the emphasis that rates do not need to react one-for-one with energy prices, that financial conditions have tightened significantly, and that we are still in a measured-adjustment scenario. Beyond that, communication will need to keep an implicit hiking bias given the more persistent shock and the fact that September forecasts were consistent with a bit more action from the ECB. At the same time, the emphasis will remain on heightened uncertainty, data-dependence, no pre-committing, and the need to decide meeting by meeting. Finally, Lagarde will need to somehow address the elephant in the room: long-term rates and spreads. We think it’s too early for any action but we would not be surprised to see some soft form of verbal intervention already. That could come in the form of a reminder that the ECB has tools to address deviations from fundamentals. It could also involve a suggestion that QT could be temporarily paused if market conditions were to remain volatile and disorderly for a while. As a reminder, we expect one final hike in December. records.text: M Update Morgan Stanley Research 3 What next? UK growth outperformance in recent months has been driven by business-to-business services, and these remain key going into 2027. But it is fair to say that even the consumer surprised a bit to the upside, reducing their savings rate in 1H and thus smoothing their consumption. Retail sector has been a particular beneficiary of this, with consumers increasing their purchases in response to frequent discounting. Perhaps the key reason why consumers decided to smooth their consumption following the immediate energy spike was the impression that the rise in fuel prices would be temporary. Fast forward 6 months later, auto fuel prices are still rising, heating bills have increased in October, and another ~20% rise is coming in January. Some re-entrenchment is likely, with, we think, an uptick in the savings rate in 4Q. Since real disposable income growth in the UK is flat to mildly negative this year, higher discretionary savings mean a slowdown in household spending. The true bull case for the UK economy is one where following the translation of stronger growth into a more stable labour market, consumers and corporates start to re-leverage. We are, however, big believers in the potency of monetary policy. We struggle to see this happening at these policy settings. records.text: aying down the A-1 tranche first, A-1 tranche investors benefit with greater protection from extension risk. Furthermore, because the A-1 tranche carries the lowest interest rate in the deal and is the largest tranche in the deal, paying it off first leaves more expensive debt behind. This accelerates the rise in the issuer’s average borrowing cost compared to a modified sequential structure, strengthening the financial incentive to call the deal before the scheduled coupon step-up takes effect. That said, this comes at the expense of the A-2 and A-3 tranches, as investors must wait longer for their respective principal repayments. Specifically, the WAL on these two tranches extends up to four years in the sequential structure, largely aligning with the expected call and principal return at the coupon step-up date (Exhibit 5). In a fully extended scenario, where the deal is not called, the lengthening in the WAL on the A-2 and A-3 tranches becomes more pronounced (again, Exhibit 5). Because mezzanine and subordinate tranches are locked out until the senior tranches have been paid down, their WAL is structurally unaffected by how the senior principal is distributed. All else equal, this longer duration should result in marginally wider A-2 and A-3 spreads relative to the A-1. Second, at his post-September meeting press conference, Governor Ueda mentioned that financial conditions would relatively tighten along with policy rate hikes, and that the BOJ is closely monitoring the impact of financial conditions on interest rates, bank lending, and asset prices. We think this indicates vigilance against excessive rate hikes. We are keen to confirm Governor Ueda’s comments on this point. Third is the Bank’s current assessment of underlying inflation. The vacancy rate held steady at 7.3% in Q2, marking a pause in its post- pandemic upward march. Slower immigration and population growth should soften rental demand, although a moderating construction pipeline could keep a lid on vacancies and affordability constraints can keep households renting. We expect the seasonally-adjusted homeownership rate to hold steady following the second-quarter decline to 65.2% from 65.4% in Q1.  Upside: A surprise uptick in rental vacancies would point to weaker market rent growth and further shelter disinflation ahead.  Downside: A decline in rental vacancies, paired with soft homeownership rates, would imply affordability constraints are contributing to firmer rental demand, while indicating headwinds for home prices. Therefore, the final major test of the cycle is Brazil’s 25 Oct 2026 runoff, where expectations about fis- cal governance clarity and the economic team are likely to matter as much for markets as campaign messaging alone. Some themes cut across the cycle. Anti-incumbency is an increasingly powerful movement, one that seems to have gained traction as public security moved from a social con- cern to a powerful electoral narrative, benefiting candidates able to link enforcement with broader institutional change. Geopolitics are also more present, with U.S. alignment increasingly salient to domestic mandates and market narra- tives, notably in Argentina and Colombia. Despite the cycle’s peculiarities, the region’s underlying eco- nomic challenges remain unchanged. For markets, the main distinction between outcomes comes from the combination of policy direction, the strength of the electoral mandate, and the capacity to implement reforms through Congress and institu- tions. Latin America still needs to sustainably raise invest- ment and productivity while addressing persistent fiscal con- straints.Now, the region faces those longstanding problems alongside a more complex global financial environment, geo- political realignment, and rapid technological change. The upshot of the CBB's survey is an increasingly mounting sign of pressure on Bahrain's economy. While the swap line was drawn by $1.67bn, reserves increased by just $776mn, which would suggest an excess of $893mn that may have been directly drained to defend the dinar's peg. What's more, with just $2.08bn of the swap line remaining and the two drawdowns in July and September roughly equal to $1.7bn, it would suggest that there is just one month's worth of the swap line left to use. At the same time, while reserves increased, at just $2.35bn these cover just 1.2 months worth of imports. Additionally, the trend of July-August-September suggests that in October the CBB would use its reserves rather than the swap line, and if the reserves are drawn down by the same amount as in August it would take them to just $1.4bn in October - the lowest level they would ever have reached. As the non-oil trade deficit also is widening, the pressure on Bahrain is increasingly mounting and we maintain that it remains a matter of when, not if, the Gulf provides financial assistance akin to the deal in 2018 (see Bahrain: war or not, Bahrain's twin balance sheet vulnerabilities need to be more firmly addressed, 28 July 2026). 23 October 2026 64 Barclays | Global Economics Weekly: When AI angst meets oil trouble

Taken together, while the near-term Budget outcome may be supportive, the medium-term fiscal and supply outlook remains less favourable and subject to considerable uncertainty, in our view. Overall, we see relatively muted risks from the Budget itself. Gilt yields should remain primarily driven by global factors, alongside the inflationary implications of the announced measures, the National Living Wage decision and the broader economic outlook. However, an unsupportive Budget could undermine the recent improvement in the relative appeal of gilts as safe-haven assets. ASWs could be more sensitive to the fiscal and supply projections. At the front end, recent tightening, potentially lighter positioning and a favourable structural demand outlook make wideners look attractive, in our view, although we see limited direct implications from the Budget itself. At the long end, a reduction in planned issuance should provide some support at the margin. However, this appears largely anticipated by the market, leaving valuations more vulnerable to disappointment should the announced remit fall short of expectations. More broadly, the Budget could still surprise on several fronts, and we remain sceptical that the medium-term fiscal and supply outlook will ultimately prove supportive for gilts and the broader ASW complex. The JSDA’s trading flow data for September showed insurers buying up super-long JGBs for a fourth straight month with their net purchases the highest in some time at around JPY500 billion (see Exhibit 3). Earlier in the year they had been net sellers while seemingly switching from off-the-run to on-the-run bonds as yields moved higher. However, cumulative net purchases since the start of the last fiscal year are now close to zero, suggesting that portfolio substitutions may now have been largely completed and that demand might accordingly taper off if yields keep declining. From a regulatory perspective lifers will have no particular need to take on additional duration when yields are falling, considering also that many might now be “over-hedged” on the asset side after suffering an increase in policy cancellations as interest rates moved higher (see Exhibit 4). Rather, the clearest explanation for a rate hike would be if their new forecasting model (PRIMA) – used for the first time in October forecasts – implied stronger upcoming energy price pass through. Officials may judge that higher rates are necessary now in order to lean against these risks, even before seeing the pass through realized. In this scenario, we think a hike could be framed somewhat dovishly as a “risk management” hike, with officials inclined to wait and see how higher rates impact the economy before hiking again (not in December). We do see net hawkish risks of higher inflation forecasts from the new PRIMA model, but with elevated uncertainty. The new model is intended to better model the effect that shocks in certain sectors will have on the rest of the economy. This is different from the current top-down output-gap-based approach of considering inflation risks. It is not clear to us if there will still be estimates of the output gap under the new model. For now, we will be a bit cautious around basing our expectations of future core inflation on the BoC’s new forecasting models. Reduced leverage demand from hedge funds has likely reduced an important source of money creation. In overnight markets, much of the attention has focused on the sharp decline in leverage demand, which is partly a consequence of SLR reform (Figure 3). But an important downstream consequence is that money fund cash recycled through dealers and hedge funds is no longer generating the same volume of secondary MMF inflows. To understand this mechanism, it is useful to consider a simple Treasury cash-futures basis trade financed through dealer repo (Figure 4). First, an MMF lends cash to a dealer, which in turn finances a leveraged Treasury position at a hedge fund. Because the trade is leveraged, the hedge fund uses borrowed funding to acquire the cash Treasury position. The seller of that Treasury security now receives cash, which must ultimately be held either as a bank deposit or invested in an MMF. In this way, hedge fund leverage creates additional cash balances that can find their way back into money funds. With basis-trade activity no longer expanding materially, this money-creation channel appears to have weakened. FIGURE 3. [Sanjay Raja]: We expect two 25-basis-point "insurance hikes"—one in November and one in February—raising the Bank Rate from 3.75% to 4.25%. These hikes are driven by persistent energy inflation. Headline CPI is expected to rise above 4%, approaching 4.5% in Q1 next year, which presents an uncomfortable backdrop. However, we are not seeing signs of deeply entrenched inflation spilling over into the wider CPI basket. In the recent September inflation print, headline CPI outpaced the Bank's expectations by 50 basis points, but almost all of this was energy-driven. Core CPI (excluding energy and food) was only 7 basis points above forecast. Additionally, wage settlements are holding steady around 3.5% heading into 2027. This suggests the Bank of England can implement these insurance hikes without embarking on a prolonged hiking cycle. Recent communications support this. Chief Economist Hugh Pill explicitly pushed back on market pricing, expressing skepticism over a four-hike trajectory, while Governor Bailey warned the market against assuming the Bank's next moves. This suggests a terminal rate of 4.25% for this cycle. This is a reprint of A tale of two index exits, published on October 20, 2026. • Index exits matter far more for high yield than investment grade corporate bond index liquidity. We track monthly turnover around Bloomberg US Corporate IG and HY index exclusions, covering six months before and after exit between 2019 and 2026. • Investment grade liquidity tends to be resilient after exclusions. Monthly turnover nearly triples from around 5% before exclusions to almost 14% in the month of removal, before stabilising at roughly 4% three months later, still broadly resilient. • High yield liquidity weakens materially after exclusions. While turnover also rises around exits in HY, the spike is far smaller than in IG. Average turnover subsequent to exits tends to fall from around 9% pre-exit to roughly 5% post-exit, a decline of nearly 50%. • Index eligibility helps explain the divergence... While financial conditions have tightened, the Fed may conclude financial conditions not have tightened sufficiently enough to support the timelier return to the Committee's 2% goal. Indeed, on October 15, Cleveland Fed President Hammack assessed that financial conditions appear roughly neutral now amid investments in things like technology that are going full speed ahead despite rising borrowing costs: "I'm not feeling that there's restraint coming from financial conditions at this…point in time." If the FOMC agrees to hike or outcome of the October meeting skews hawkish, we believe investors think less about how high rates need to remain to control inflation and more about how far rates eventually fall due to growth consequences of keeping them there. Although this spread has flattened as cracks in risky assets become more visible, we think market pricing still implies too little easing between the peak and trough of the cycle. • This spread sits at -24bp, vs. an historical average of -131bp (see Exhibit 3 ). This setup is more favorable for real rate longs in the US, where fading inflation n pressures should provide greater relief in policy pricing and real rates. More persistent inflation is a risk that could limit dovish policy repricing, but it does not necessarily preclude real rate outperformance versus nominals. Despite real yields doing the heavy lifting in this year’s selloff, TIPS have delivered better returns than nominals as inflation has exceeded market pricing. Instead, the clearest risk to real yields meaningfully underperforming is growth-led disinflation, which typically sees nominal longs more clearly outperform. In Europe, this backdrop argues more for a short inflation bias, either outright or n via nominal longs, given richer inflation pricing relative to both our economists’ forecasts and model-implied fair value. Near-dated nominal forwards such as 1y1y or 1y2y could offer a way to capture both less hawkish policy expectations sustained by easing inflation risks. Reassessing our positioning Strong economic momentum and idiosyncratic risks pose headwinds for the front end and reduce the appeal of steepeners UK rates came under meaningful flattening pressure over the past week (see Exhibit 10) , with front-end rates trading particularly weak and the strip actually selling off and underperforming on a cross-market basis, especially compared to the US (see Exhibit 11). Among the main reasons were stronger-than-expected labour market data, particularly higher payrolls and a lower unemployment rate, alongside stronger PMIs. Additionally, the ONS release of the Annual Survey of Hours and Earnings (ASHE), which showed median hourly earnings for full-time employees (excluding overtime) rising by 5.7% y/y in the year to April 2026, poses a further headwind to the UK front end. Our economists now see a risk of the National Living Wage (NLW) being raised by 5.5%, compared with around 4% previously expected. This will be a key factor to watch at the upcoming Budget, as it could add hawkish risks to the BoE's reaction function and put further pressure on the UK front end.

records.text: ntributing a combined 1pp to y/y core inflation. Meanwhile in Europe, energy has been the primary driver of the increase in both realized and traded inflation. Between February and September, the energy contribution to the year-over-year rate of headline inflation increased by around 2pp in the Euro Area and 0.9pp in the UK. Alongside other fundamental factors, these pressures have pushed nominal yields higher across the G3 this year, though the relative contributions from inflation and real yields have differed materially. In Europe and the UK, higher energy prices have driven a significant repricing in front-end inflation, with little contribution from higher real rates. In the US, by contrast, front-end inflation risks mostly translated directly into higher real yields and a much more hawkish expected policy path (Exhibit 1). Several factors may explain this divergence. The US benefits from a larger AI-related growth tailwind, and we find that higher consensus forecasts for long-run GDP growth account for a large share of the rise in US yields this year (Exhibit 2). In Europe and the UK, by contrast, a softer underlying growth backdrop and the recently dominant “circuit breaker” of wider sovereign spreads may be constraining both real yields and the degree of policy tightening that the market can sustainably price. 23 October 2026 2 Goldman Sachs Global Markets Daily For the exclusive use of CAYLA.BUETTNER@BLUECRESTCAPITAL.COM 7595159db82544668b3260609400172c

records.text: US Credit Alpha Overview Hyperscalers' revenue is strong, but capex keeps rising. The financing game theory has been spelled out: raise early before others absorb the capital, but avoid too much debt on the balance sheet. Markets haven't taken that well. We expect AI supply to keep a lid on short-term spread tightening. Prisoner’s dilemma spooks the markets Great revenue, but more capex. Meta's 3Q showed the same pattern as other hyperscalers recently. Revenue growth is materializing, but capex is also increasing, and spending ambitions appear higher (see here). The central question is not whether the AI build-out will be funded, but who will fund it, how, and how fast. Meta has made the prisoner's dilemma explicit. In its filing, Meta's special committee said that timing matters. Recent and expected raises at other companies in the AI ecosystem have made raising capital "increasingly challenging. " Meta has enough capital for today's needs, but the committee judged it prudent to raise before others absorb more of the available capital. Each company has an incentive to move first, so supply is front-loaded. The collective result is higher funding costs for everyone in the AI complex, and that means wider new-issue concessions across AI-linked credit and pressure on the indices too. But too much debt on the balance sheet is not optimal, so equity or off-balance-sheet funding steps in. Meta’s committee also concluded that debt of the size management was considering could hurt r

records.text: 23 October 2026 UK Weekly Digest Deutsche Bank AG Page 7 Credit: After a record-breaking August, we expect net consumer credit to cool a touch in September (August: GBP 2.5bn). We expect net consumer credit to have slipped to GBP 2bn in September. Sales volumes fell by 0.4% m-o-m, and by more than expected. The GfK consumer confidence data also slipped by 10pts to -24 in September – marking the largest single month drop since the pandemic . This, we think, should take some of the heat out of credit card borrowing. But don't expect a collapse. Car dealership finance should keep "other" consumer credit ticking along. The September plate change was the strongest since 2017, with registrations up 12% y -o-y and private demand up close to 14%. Chunky manufacturer discount s, the Electric Car Grant and high pump prices pushed buyers towards new EVs. Fuel volumes also rose 2.2% m -o-m at elevated prices, which adds to card balances at the margin. Net consumer credit has beaten expectations in every month so far this year. And with real wages squeezed by the energy shock, the risk is that households lean on credit more. On mortgage approvals, we expect another drop to 5 4k. Swap rates climbed through September as markets priced in a hike, and lenders kept repricing. The average two -year fix jumped by around 25bp over the month, and fixes priced below 5% have all but vanished – from nearly 1,500 at the start of September to just nine by early October. The surveys tell the same story.

records.text: CP declining to 4.9%Y (from 5.0%Y) and headline CPI slightly lower at 4.8%Y (from 4.9%Y). We think energy prices should remain broadly flat (0.2%M) over the month. Electricity prices are likely to rise (2.0%M), but this should be more than offset by lower fuels and lubricants (-2.1%M), supported by the extension of the government’s energy measures until year-end and the associated increase in petrol discounts to 20ct/L from 5ct/L in September. At the same time, gas prices should rise this month (~7%M) following the quarterly update to regulated market prices, which cover around one third of the market. However, here again, government measures are cushioning the increase for consumers, limiting the rise in the regulated market to only 17%M (see here) instead of 54%M otherwise (see here). It is important to note that the gas measure is not a subsidy, but rather aims to smooth the price adjustment over time, which will keep prices more elevated well into 2027. The remaining two thirds of consumers are on the free market and typically benefit from fixed tariffs, meaning prices are likely to be rising only marginally by comparison. When it comes to core HICP the data has proved more robust than we previously expected. For October, we see it remaining unchanged at 3.5%Y, but we are attentive to any upside surprise, particularly from services, as a gauge of the country’s underlying inflation momentum going forward.

The first 20-day customs exports rose 105.4% oya, and after adjusting for working-day differences we estimate full-month export growth at 82.4% oya. On our seasonal adjustment, 20-day exports increased 7.0% m/m sa—materi- ally better than the -1.8% m/m sa first-10-day read and simi- lar to the pattern seen in July. On this trajectory, it is increas- ingly plausible that seasonally adjusted exports will rise again on a full-month basis in October; if so, the three-month trend could re-accelerate towards ~100% saar (Figure 2). The real-side message remains equally important. The BoK’s export volume index rose 5.6% m/m sa in September for a second consecutive month, leaving 3Q export volume growth at 43.8% ar—close to the pace seen in 1Q. records.text: M Idea 2 US Economics: Key views US Economic Outlook: Resilience meets Restraint Growth: Resilient despite adverse trade and oil shocks. Real GDP grows 2.4% (4Q/4Q) in 2026 and 2.3% in 2027. Final private domestic demand is even stronger but slows modestly into next year. Labor: Low hire/low fire. Employment remains soft, but immigration controls have reduced breakevens to ~50k per month. Despite a low unemployment rate, wage growth is decelerating. Signs of overheating are scarce. Inflation: A sticky path lower. We expect disinflation, but second-round effects from the oil shock and residual seasonality mean slow progress. Core PCE ends 2026 at 3.1% (4Q/4Q) and 2027 at 2.6%. Consumer: Resilient, with two-speeds. Low-income consumers remain squeezed, while wealth supports the high end. Real consumption slows to 1.8% in 2027 from 2.3% in 2026. AI: Increasingly macro-relevant. AI-related investment contributes around 60bps to real GDP growth in 2026 and 2027. AI-driven productivity growth adds a further boost. Labor displacement is modest. Fed: Measured tightening. We expect two 25bp hikes in December and March, to a target range of 4.25%-4.5%. Data support a measured recalibration of Fed policy over more aggressive tightening.

records.text: Core inflation ticked up to 2.5% in September—driven by firmer services inflation—and our summary indicator of underlying inflation—which averages over eight exclusion- and model-based measures—stood at 2.7% on a three-month annualised basis (Exhibit 1, right). But wage measures have remained more contained, with Indeed posted wage growth falling back to 2.6%, towards the lower end of the 2.5-3% range that we estimate to be consistent with 2% inflation. The ECB will have access to its surveys (including SAFE, the Corporate Telephone Survey and the Survey of Professional Forecasters) for an updated picture on second-round wage pressures for the meeting. Turning to market developments, spot and forward energy prices have continued to rise. The 60/40 average of Brent oil and TTF natural gas prices—which reflects the relative weight of each in the consumption basket after accounting for passthrough to other components—is up 50% since the cut-o ff date for the September ECB projections, with forwards in between the staff’s adverse and severe scenarios (Exhibit 2, left). This points to upward pressure on the staff’s inflation projection for 2027. records.text: e widening beyond a point. With rates now falling and our bias to be long duration, we think the dynamics that pushed the basis wider are likely to reverse, creating scope for the basis to tighten, especially given the asymmetric bias of mortgage convexity to the downside (See "Convexity driven moves have an endpoint"). Why does the basis exist? The CME-LCH basis is the difference between pay fixed rates on benchmark interest rates swaps with the exact same maturity that clear on CME and LCH's swap clearing facilities respectively. While this may appear to be a violation of the "no-arbitrage" rule, it reflects the segmentation of the cleared swaps market, and emerges when the positioning of market participants clearing on CME (typically some US asset managers paying fixed) ends up being dramatically different from the positioning that dominates at LCH (other market participants, many large global banks and swap dealers). Asset managers paying fixed at CME causes dealers to receive fixed there, when their natural netting efficiency from legacy books incentivizes them to receive fixed on LCH. Although the two positions are exactly the same from a rates perspective (leaving no rates market impact), paying flows on CME create netting inefficiency, which allows for a small basis to emerge and persist. The deterioration in sentiment was broad-based - it happened across different income and age brackets, and it reflected a decline in major purchases intentions, greater readiness to save, and more pessimism around both personal financial and general economic prospects. Unemployment expectations went up and so did inflation expectations. The headline consumer confidence number these days is a simple beta to inflation expectations - as these go up, in tandem with headline inflation, the general consumer sentiment sours. This is why we tend to disagree with the recommendations for a small targeted (fiscal) package of household energy bills support. Given the BoE is focused primarily on spot data, the optimal policy intervention, we think, is generalised support aimed at reducing inflation - and funded by fiscal revenue raising measures elsewhere (i.e. not borrowing). The boost to growth is thus primarily delivered via less tight financial conditions than would otherwise be the case and, of course, via lower inflation.

The case for holding in October rests mainly on the Committee's prior signaling of no urgency to tighten (from Williams, Jefferson, Bowman, and Daly, among others), reinforced by Chairman Warsh's own silence on the question at the IMF meetings last week, which did so little to lean against October hold expectations that fed funds futures markets lowered the implied hike probability about 12pp (to roughly 15%). The focus is not limited to the amount of deposit outflows. Banks will be tested on how much interest they need to pay to retain deposits. In principle, Retail Government Bond Plus cannot be redeemed during the first year after issuance. Corporate funds moving into JGBs are therefore likely to consist mainly of surplus funds with no near-term use, rather than funds for daily settlement. Accordingly, the total cash & deposits held by companies should not be viewed directly as the potential amount of outflows. However, more investment options could prompt increases in deposit rates and a shift from low-cost liquid deposits to term deposits. For banks, maintaining deposit balances does not necessarily protect net interest income. From a top-down perspective, we expect stronger differentiation among banks based on factors including deposit franchises and the ability to pass higher rates through to lending rates.

Optimism about long-end auction size reductions Growing speculation that the Treasury could reduce long-end auction sizes or even eliminate 20s altogether has also helped support long-end spreads. However, we see little reason (see here) for the Treasury to make adjustments in November. The August refunding guidance "anticipates maintaining nominal coupon and FRN auction sizes for at least the next several quarters. " We see little reason for the Treasury to deviate from that guidance. Although long- end yields have risen, much of the move reflects higher expected policy rates rather than term premium. At the same time, a flatter Treasury curve and wider long-end spreads have improved the relative economics of issuing at the long end. And so the cost of issuing at the long-end has not increased as much as the increase in outright yields would suggest. As a result, we expect auction sizes to remain unchanged in November, though the Treasury may modestly tweak its forward guidance to preserve greater flexibility over the timing and composition of future issuance. 23 October 2026 4 Barclays | Interest Rate Derivatives

A reduction in Fed purchases implies larger privately-held net marketable borrowing needs all else equal. The tripling of long-end liquidity support buybacks has also added to financing needs in the current quarter. Lastly, we think Treasury will assume a cash balance of $850bn at the end of December, $134bn lower than where it stood at the end of September, and a cash balance of $950bn at the end of March, consistent with its cash management policy. On net, we project Treasury will announce $635bn of privately-held net marketable borrowing needs in the October-December quarter, and $771bn in the January-March quarter. It's worth noting that with public debt outstanding sitting just $1.12tn below the statutory limit as of September, the debt limit is expected to become binding next quarter, if legislation is not passed in a timely manner. Once the debt limit becomes binding, Treasury can use extraordinary measures and its cash balance in order to meet financing needs, which would likely last until late summer or early fall. Higher freight costs are being absorbed partly through lower FOB prices— particularly for barrels traveling longer distances—while refiners still face sharply higher delivered costs (Figure 7). The result is a market in which crude can become more expensive for the buyer even as it becomes less valuable to the producer. But does this explain why Brent is trading nearly $20 above its fundamental value? Our analysis suggests not. Despite the extraordinary increase in freight costs, we find no evidence of material freight pass-through into either Brent futures or Dated Brent. The adjustment is occuring primarily through physical crude differentials, rather than through the benchmarks themselves. This leaves geopolitical risk as the more plausible explanation for Brent’s premium over fair value. Geography is reshaping the relative value of crude around the world, but it does not explain why the benchmark itself remains so elevated. The distinction matters: one reflects the cost of moving oil today. The other reflects what the market is willing to pay for the possibility that tomorrow’s supply may once again be disrupted. European Natural Gas: How the El Niño can steal winter The impact of El Niño is potentially bearish for natural gas through lower heating and power demand, given warmer, wetter and windier weather conditions. Current weather forecasts for Europe point to a materially warmer winter, with Nov-Dec 1.4stdev warmer (vs 10-yr normal) and Jan-Feb 0.5stdev warmer. If realized, this could lift end-March storage by up to 6%-pt versus 10-year normal assumptions, all else equal. More favorable wind and hydro conditions could provide a further 9%-pt impact on end-March storage level. Despite the significantly warmer winter outlook, especially for the first half of the season, we incorporate only a modest adjustment given the inherent uncertainty around seasonal forecasts. For now, we model November as around 0.7 stdev warmer and December as 0.5 stdev warmer, compared with current forecasts of around 1.4 stdev warmer. We keep January-March in line with the 10-year average. We do not currently incorporate any potential El Niño impact on wind and hydro generation, or the related effect on thermal generation and gas burn. If realized, these factors would add further bearishness to our balances. This was due to a slowdown in both services and manufacturing. On a country basis, Germany and the rest of the Eurozone registered slower, but still positive growth, while France fell into contraction territory. As regards the sectoral breakdown, the Services PMI fell 1.3 points to a 2- month low of 51.7 with declines across employment, new business and business expectations. The Manufacturing PMI declined 0.5 points to a 3-month low of 52.4 with the details for output, new orders and employment also on the weak side. Despite elevated energy prices, aggregate input prices rose by only 0.3pp to 67.3, while output prices surprisingly declined by 1.2 points to 67.3. October PMI is the first data point for Q4 and, at 51.9, is below the Q3 average at 52.4, signalling activity slowdown into year- end. Eurozone Q3 GDP will be released on 31 October, we expect a rate of 0.2% q/q, followed by 0.3% in Q4. When interpreting today's data, we would once again point to the significant underperformance of France, while the rest of the Eurozone saw less of a setback, despite higher energy prices.
