October PMIs point to resilient growth Very short-end yields are likely to continue to feel pressure from central bank policy rates, as the higher energy costs and the for now still-robust demand imply persisting inflation pressures. Incoming growth signals still support the narrative of resilient economic activity, including the most recent PMIs. In the US, the flash S&P Global composite PMI was little changed at 57.6 in October (manufacturing 56.0, services 57.9), which we interpret as consistent with continued above- trend growth heading into Q4. Mirroring the strength, in the UK, the composite PMI accelerated to 53.1, up from 52.0 in September. The press release cited that demand conditions were buoyed by increased sales from AI investment and increased demand for technology services, alongside robust global economic conditions. In the euro area, the composite PMI declined 1.2pt, to 51.9, reflecting slower growth in services and manufacturing output. The signals point to some moderation in underlying activity, albeit at still-resilient levels. However, input cost pressures intensified further (+0.3pt, to 67.3), although firms continue to show evidence of margin compression, with overall output price pressures slowing (-1.2pt to 55.5). Dollar performance was mixed, and generally n contained, in an otherwise challenging week for markets. This week’s performance reinforces a few common elements that have prevailed in FX for much of the year. First, terms of trade have continued to be a strong driver of returns under the surface of the major crosses. This week’s top performers— including AUD, CAD and NOK—all bene fit from higher energy prices and policy expectations have also drifted in this direction. Crosses like NOK/SEK help demonstrate that, while volatility in the major Dollar crosses has been mostly subdued, the moves in energy importers vs exporters have been anything but. And, when we expand beyond commodities, countries where the terms of trade have improved via AI demand, like KRW, have also seen a clear currency benefit and remained resilient lately even as the market debates the durability of the causal energy and AI price surges. Second, we believe the market’s assessment of future capital expenditures has been driving the broad Dollar direction. This helps explain both the shifting correlation of FX to energy prices and the Dollar’s more procyclical properties lately. Third, overall FX volatility remains subdued while there are limited signs of divergence or pressing recession concerns. The Outlook Report is likely to contain only modest revisions, with growth forecasts broadly unchanged and inflation projections revised slightly higher, reflecting yen appreciation and developments in energy prices. records.text: Emerging Asia Outlook Leaning hawkish The BSP surprised with a 50bp rate hike earlier this week, we expect another in December. The BoK's pause was expected, but the commentary was hawkish. The RBI may likely raise the policy rate again in December. Not all central banks are looking to tighten policy though, as indicated by BI's pause. Inflation concerns driving more rate hikes Monetary policy divergence in EM Asia is once again coming to the fore, with select central banks likely to tighten policy further, given inflation (BSP , RBI) and financial stability (BoK) concerns. On the other end of the spectrum, select central banks are unlikely to tighten policy settings again (MAS) or remain accommodative through this year (BoT). The differences in policy paths are attributable to growth-inflation dynamic, the reaction functions of the central banks and the priority order they assign to policy objectives: The BSP is the most sensitive to high inflation in the region. The RBI, as an inflation-targeting central bank, has also begun its tightening cycle, as it found rising inflationary pressures difficult to ignore. While BI has historically raised rates in response to IDR depreciation pressures, its recent decision to pause suggests it hopes these pressures are transitory. In contrast, the BoT has been the most dovish in the region, prioritising supporting growth and maintaining policy rate unchanged so far in the year, in line with its historical reaction function. Concerns over the creditworthiness of AI cloud companies also weighed on market sentiment. Underlying this is the question of how far massive AI data center investment will translate into earnings and whether the investment will generate adequate returns. Meanwhile, the US 10-year Treasury yield has declined. This indicates that the correction reflected not only inflation concerns but also a reassessment of growth expectations supported by AI investment. However, it would be premature to interpret this reassessment as an immediate sign of recession. According to estimates by our US equity strategy team and GVAT team, YoY growth in AI- related capex, including leases, is expected to slow from around 100% in 2026 to around 60% in 2027 and around 14% in 2028. Russian Urals has traditionally been priced on both a free-on-board (FOB) basis at Russian export terminals—where the buyer covers delivery costs—and on a delivered basis, including cost, insurance and freight (CIF) at destination ports—where the producer pays the expenses. Historically, however, it made little difference to the overall crude price: freight from Russia to Europe was typically only around $2 per barrel. Since Western sanctions redirected Russian exports toward Asia, opaque shipping arrangements, intermediary margins and sanctions-related costs have made it increasingly difficult to determine how much producers actually receive. Most Middle Eastern crudes are assessed through yet another mechanism. Saudi grades, Iraq’s Basrah and Kuwait Export Crude are more commonly sold under term contracts using official selling prices (OSPs). Rather than negotiating a fixed outright price for each cargo, producers typically set a monthly premium or discount to a regional benchmark—generally Oman/Dubai for Asian buyers, and often Dated Brent (or a related Brent reference) for European buyers. Source: Citi Research Source: Citi Research, Bloomberg Belly rate tends to outperform: 3m fwd 2s5s bull flattener In terms of the broader economy, we believe that the level of real yield after the September sell-off could already be somewhat restrictive on growth, and the housing sector appears to show some signs of a slowdown as a result. The pending home sales data released this week shows a sharp decline of -7.3% MoM, and typically outsized declines such as this have coincided with meaningful increases in yields, as one would expect (Figure 7). Over the past 20 years (excluding the GFC and Covid in 2020), declines in pending home sales of equivalent magnitude or more have happened only 5 times and the front end of the yield curve (2s5s) has generally flattened (by 9.7bps on average) over the subsequent month in those cases (Figure 8). We believe this is likely due to the market pricing for an increased chance of an economic slowdown and the need for the Fed to ease not immediately but later down the road. The 2007 data point was the clear exception with the 2s5s curve steepening because the Fed was already cutting rates aggressively that same month. Obviously, the current environment is not analogous to 2007 given that the market is still pricing for Fed hikes. Similarly, the belly of the 2s5s30s Tsy fly also tends to outperform the wings (the fly tightened by 8bps on average) over the month immediately following the sharp declines

records.text: US Economics Weekly 23 October 2026 ab 4 High gas prices versus tax cuts? Boost or burden? In a paper presented at the Brookings Institution in September, “ From Importer to Exporter: Oil Shocks and the U.S. Economy ,” three economists, including the well known econometrician James Stock, argued that the impact of higher energy prices on the US Economy is essentially zero, or even positive. That result is not all that new. For example, a paper presented at Brookings exactly a decade earlier found that an oil price increase had no net negative effect on US growth because the investment response to the oil price increase would offset the drag of higher energy prices on consumption. (1) However, what was new about the paper presented this year was that higher energy prices had no net negative impact on real personal consumption expenditures. In other words, growth was insensitive to a rise in oil prices even if there were no meaningful positive response from US investment in new drilling. Although we are somewhat sceptical about the empirical identification of that result, that result of no impact on consumer spending from high gas prices is itself a comment on how insensitive the US economy has become to energy price shocks.In our analysis and projection, we estimate the direct impact of higher energy prices is small but not quite zero, and assume potential spillover effects weigh on broader spending. records.text: 23 October 2026 Euro Weekly Digest Deutsche Bank AG Page 2 Inflation: Rising energy prices have pushed up headline HICP inflation to 3.8% yoy (Sep). HICP inflation is expected to rise to c.4.0% in Q4, before declining in 2027. We are not yet seeing signs of the energy spilling over into the broader inflation basket, but core inflation (2.5%) has proven sticky in 2026, especially due to consumer electronics prices, and the latest household inflation expectations print showed a sharp rise, highlighting the risk of future second-round effects. Growth: We continue to view GDP growth as resilient, and the economy appears to be absorbing the energy shock well. But mixed signals from the data question whether the resilience is temporary or persistent . We continue to see growth picking up from 0.8% this year, to 1.2% in 2027 and 1.3% in 2028 – around trend. Monetary Policy: We expect a final ECB hike to 2.75% in December, with risks of a further hike to 3%. With core inflation sticky and the economy resilient, a mildly restrictive stance is appropriate. The ECB has started again describing the policy response as “measured” (we think that means a quarterly pace of hikes, and rates only going to mildly restrictive). Rising global yields and tighter financial conditions are crowding out the need for the ECB to hike as far as the market had initially priced (recent ECB commentary also hinted at this). This week’s developments remind us of the weeks ahead of the June 2023 rate hike (when consensus was for rates unchanged) and of the weeks ahead of the October 2022 50bp hike (as opposed to 75bp consensus). In both instances, somewhat stale comments from BoC officials led markets to price the upcoming meeting in one direction, while data indicated something else. As officials make policy decisions as one unified body, intermeeting comments that stick to prior messaging are not necessarily intended to provide new guidance. The signal provided by the data was the better indication of what officials actually decided in both June 2023 and October 2022. Both instances were also a notable surprise relative to market pricing at the time (one a hawkish surprise, one a dovish surprise). China therefore faces three transitions simultaneously: AI and technology, green investment, and investment to consumption. The third is critical. Industrial upgrading can strengthen productivity and competitiveness without generating enough employment and household income to offset persistently weak domestic demand. Monetary policy alone cannot bridge that gap. Conventional rate cuts are becoming less powerful. In a deleveraging environment, cheaper money does not automatically create credit demand. Hence, the PBoC is increasingly relying on targeted credit and structural monetary tools. Central government has a bigger role to play in supporting domestic demand, while local governments remain under debt consolidation mandates, leading to a de-facto contraction that offsets the central government’s expansionary fiscal guidance. China retains capacity to support households and consumption, but policy priorities continue to favour industrial capability, technology self-reliance and supply-chain resilience. records.text: d Brent (or a related Brent reference) for European buyers. That structure makes OSPs particularly hard to interpret. Unlike a freely traded spot price, an OSP is set by the producer and reflects a blend of market conditions, competing crude grades, refinery economics, and commercial strategy. A reduction in the OSP differential may signal weakening demand, but it could just as easily represent an attempt to protect market share or compensate buyers for higher transportation costs. We began to see this dynamic in early July 2026. After the US signed the MoU with Iran, more Hormuz-linked barrels flowed back into the market, but buying remained cautious. Producers therefore had to compete more aggressively for market share in Asia. Saudi Arabia’s July 6 announcement underscored that shift. It set some of the deepest discounts for August deliveries to Asian buyers—levels comparable only to the COVID period—and the month-on-month cut was described as the steepest in roughly two decades. By October, those discounts had widened further, moving from roughly $3 to $7 versus Dubai for November delivery across different grades—a $14/bbl swing in the differential in just four months (Figure 1). The basis is directional from time to time because an important part of the activity on CME appears to be related to the hedging of mortgage convexity specific to US rates markets. When rates rise, mortgage duration extends and negatively convex investors need to shed duration, including by paying fixed in swaps. To the extent that this flow is disproportionately cleared at CME, the cross-CCP imbalance grows and the basis widens. In particular, a large or rapid sell-off of the kind that occurred in September can generate a more concentrated wave of paying fixed in swaps, as was also evidenced by the widening in swap spreads. This dynamic explains why the CME-LCH basis widened in the sell-off. Over the short term, the mechanism also works in reverse when rates decline. Mortgage duration shortens, the need to pay fixed declines and prior pay fixed hedges may need to be unwound. This reduces the imbalance between CME and LCH swaps and puts downward pressure on the basis. There are already early signs of this occurring as rates have moved lower recently. The apparent differences mostly reflect the national mix of gasoline and diesel as well as domestic support measures. Meanwhile, the pass-through of higher TTF prices to retail natural gas and electricity prices is much more heterogeneous (Exhibit 9). At this stage, on a year- on-year basis it is strong in Italy, a bit less in Spain and France, and largely absent in Germany so far (where we also flag that a base effect from a grid fees subsidy in January-26 lowers the year-on-year metric). This is broadly in line with our ex-ante analysis based on previous episodes (here). On natural gas (Exhibit 10) , we note a strong and rapid pass-through in Italy and France, while more lagged in Spain. In Germany, HICP natural gas prices have barely moved so far, as higher gas costs have been largely offset by sequential declines in distribution costs. The increase in the underlying gas component has also remained more moderate than in other countries. The pattern of the pass- through to electricity (Exhibit 11) is relatively similar to that of natural gas for Italy, Spain and Germany. But it differs in France where electricity markets remain highly regulated and tariff updates are scheduled only twice a year (February and August). records.text: high-energy-price backdrop. CAD: Funding face-off. We have highlighted CAD as an appealing funding currency n for FX carry trades for much of this year despite elevated energy prices. At first glance, this seems counterintuitive given Canada’s status as an energy exporter and CAD’s ranking in our GSTOT framework as one of the largest beneficiaries of higher oil prices. We recently examined the drivers of this divergence and assessed the outlook for continuing to use CAD as a funding currency candidate for carry trades. Despite more complicated dynamics under the surface, we find that CAD’s typical relationship with oil remains intact. Considerable widening in the spread between WCS and Brent, driven in part by increased Venezuelan exports of heavy crude oil to the United States, has diluted the benefit of higher oil prices. Nonetheless, CAD has remained a consistent outperformer within G10 FX on days when oil prices rise. Instead, rate differentials have been the much more dominant driver of CAD performance, and the BoC’s slower shift towards rate hikes relative to other G10 central banks has contributed to the low carry-to-vol that is central to CAD’s appeal as a funding currency for FX carry trades. That said, following more hawkish messages from both the Q3 Business Outlook Survey and Governor Macklem at this past weekend’s IMF meetings, our economists now expect the BoC to deliver 25bp hikes at the October meeting as well as in January 2027. The combination of communication and a less favorable medium-term inflation outlook led us to change our call. Higher energy prices also provide an important offset to the inflation shock through Canada's terms of trade. As a net energy exporter, Canada benefits from higher energy prices through increased export revenues, corporate profits, and government income. The BoC's April MPR highlighted that the domestic growth benefit is likely to be smaller than in previous energy shocks, reflecting greater foreign ownership, more capital-efficient production, and a weaker investment response. Nevertheless, as higher prices persist, the income gains become more consequential, providing some support to activity even as higher gasoline and diesel prices reduce household purchasing power and raise business costs. Recent BoC communications suggest that the Bank is increasingly recognizing this growth offset, reducing the downside risks associated with tighter policy. We pencil in the second hike for January rather than December, with the risk of an earlier move if inflation shows clearer pass-through. Before the December 9th decision, the Bank will receive only one additional CPI report, October inflation, to be released on November 1

records.text: More of the same from activity data This week's trickle of indicators continued to point to solid, broad-based momentum, even as housing remained a clear laggard. The flash S&P Global composite PMI (Figure 3) was little changed at 57.6 in October (manufacturing 56.0, services 57.9), which we interpret as consistent with continued above-trend growth heading into Q4. Meanwhile, September housing starts (Figure 4) fell 5.2% m/m, to 1.221mn saar, below forecasts (Barclays: 1.350mn; consensus: 1.305mn), and the October NAHB index dropped 3pp, to 29, its lowest since June 2012. Housing weakness trimmed 0.1pp off our Q3 GDP tracker, which now sits at 2.6% q/q saar as we approach next week's advance Q3 GDP release. Lots of data next week, but too late to derail an October hold Next week's dense data slate will mostly arrive too late to inform the FOMC's decision. The advance Q3 GDP estimate and the September PCE price index are both released the day after the meeting, and the Committee typically does not see even an advance staff estimate of PCE inflation until the prior afternoon. Even if officials saw this data somewhat earlier than usual, it would be too late to derail an October hold at this stage, reinforcing our view that the decision rests primarily on signaling and timing considerations, rather than any fresh data point. Neutral rates Our assessment of the inflation outlook suggests that a mildly restrictive stance on monetary policy would be appropriate. Hence our call for a hike to 2.75% in December, with risk of a further hike to 3% in early 2027. This view assumes that 2.5% is the upper end of the range of nominal neutra l rates, as argued by ECB Chief Economist Philip Lane. There are reasons why neutral rates could be higher, such as the size of the German fiscal easing and the current global competition for capital to fund AI investment. But there is nothing to suggest the ECB is buying into these arguments yet. If they do, the path for monetary policy could be different. One way to explain market terminal rate rising to 3.25-3.50% in recent months is that the upper end of neutral is 3.00% rather than 2.50%. records.text: doing part of the ECB’s work. In this note we consider the policy -tool debate. The ECB faces two main challenges: inflation and France. We conclude that (1) policy rates remain the primary tool for adjusting the monetary stance; (2) tighter financial conditions may limit rate increases in the coming months; and (3) while inflation risks remain skewed upwards, the optimal combination is likely to be rate hikes —moderated by tighter financial conditions —and TPI, if needed, to stabilise France. This is preferable to slowing or stopping QT to address tighter financial conditions and restarting flexible PEPP reinvestments to stabilise France. The hurdle to changing QT plans is high, especially amid an inflation threat. The focus on 29 October will be communications. Parts of the policy statement and press conference could sound hawkish, particularly with energy prices rising above the September ‘adverse’ scenario. However, we expect a more balanced overall tone that leaves market pricing broadly unchanged. The key message will be the changing weights within the ECB reaction function. At the start of the energy shock, the ‘inflation outlook and risks’ dominated. The ECB can now orient its decision more towards ‘underlying inflation’ —given no evidence of indirect or second-round effects—and ‘transmission’: monetary policy tightened early, and higher global yields and tighter financial conditions , in part driven by France, are reinforcing the policy tightening. records.text: US Economics Weekly 23 October 2026 ab 29 Initial claims for unemployment insurance (Oct 24), 08:30 AM We expect initial claims rose 3K to 197K in the week ending October 24 after falling - 6K in the prior week. Steady claims in Gulf-Coast states suggest Hurricane Isaias had little impact on filings. The week including October 17 also included the October 12 federal holiday. Years with similar calendar setups showed only a slight edge up in seasonally-adjusted claims in first full week after the holiday. We expect continuing claims fell -3K to 1725K in the week ending October 17 after rising by 25K in the week ending October 10. records.text: MXN & ZAR: Shifting gears. We have often paired up ZAR and MXN as two EM n currencies that are high-beta and that offer similar carry returns, around 2.5% currently. However, they have different regional exposures—with MXN more geared towards US growth—and sensitivities to global energy price shifts—where ZAR is more vulnerable. These differences together with the Peso’s higher carry-to-vol led us to prefer MXN carry through most of the year, despite its less attractive valuation. However, the skew of risks has been shifting in the opposite direction. This started with concerns about a potential US diesel export ban, but has increasingly been driven by Mexico’s monetary policy. Banxico’s policy signals have been increasingly dovish against a backdrop of higher global rates, including in the US, and have a clear negative FX impact. While MXN depreciation over the past month has been sharp, the currency is flat relative to one year ago, and on the stronger side of its 5-year range. In our view, this means that policymaker urgency to support the currency is likely still some way off. records.text: BRL: High stakes into round 2. After appreciating sharply following the first round n of Brazil’s general election, BRL performance has been more mixed recently (Exhibit 3). We find this to be consistent with the impulse from global market developments as well as local factors, namely the tightening in polls ahead of this weekend’s runoff. With greater uncertainty now relative to immediately after the first round, we think a large FX market reaction to the runoff outcome is warranted. We think this is the case under both potential scenarios, albeit with larger asymmetry under a surprise incumbent victory, as currently reflected by options markets. Importantly, fiscal policy has loosened substantially in recent weeks, leaving the fiscal baseline in a worse position under a status quo outcome, and also pointing to higher hurdles to fiscal consolidation under a market-friendly outcome. Further out, cabinet appointments and policy announcements should keep volatility elevated beyond the election window. News reports have discussed the possibility of a transition bill being presented before a new administration takes office, but this may be more challenging to achieve than it was in the aftermath of the 2022 election. Seasonal outflows in December could be an added headwind to BRL if actual policy announcements disappoint, though we have found limited evidence of a structural impact of these flows on BRL performance in the past. Compared to our forecast, the main driver of the surprise was core inflation that increased 0.25%. Within that, services was the main contributor to the headline print (+13bp), mainly due to non-housing and education services (+10bp) which saw a higher contribution than in recent years. In particular, we note a strong out-of-season increase in air transport (+4bp) likely affected by higher fuel prices. It is important to remember that gasoline and diesel prices are smoothed by the government's mechanism through tax subsidy which has limited impact on consumer prices but not jet fuel costs. Other pressures came from non-core services, which were more in line with our price monitoring. As expected, this print reflected the initial seasonal adjustment in electricity tariffs as subsidies begin to be lifted, and so electricity was the top contributor to the headline print (+21bp). Despite a strong increase in husk tomato prices, agricultural products saw a more muted print as that was offset by lower prices in other food items. records.text: A sharp hedge fund derisking this week and an ongoing increase in equity n supply underscore the importance of household demand for US equities. Hedge fund gross leverage fell sharply this week but remains above the 90th percentile vs. the past 5 years. While very recent increases in retail trading activity and leveraged ETF flows have signaled an ongoing “buy the dip” mentality, retail trading volumes in US equities have declined by 20% since the summer and 45% since late 2025. Likewise, after surging in mid-2025, our Speculative Trading Indicator has turned lower in recent months. Weak consumer sentiment and elevated energy prices likely explain most of n the reduction in retail trading activity. In addition to leveraged ETFs, equity options and prediction markets have become fast-growing alternatives for retail traders. Monthly prediction market volumes have grown to $78 billion in September from $5 billion a year ago. However, this increase remains small relative to retail equity volumes, and the decline in trading activity appears broadly consistent with the recent downturns in consumer sentiment and personal saving rates alongside rising energy prices. Despite a decline in retail trading, broader household demand for US n equities has been extremely strong this year. Households directly own 42% of the US equity market and control the majority including indirect ownership via investment funds. The top 10% of households by wealth own 87% of total household equity assets.

We do, though, believe extreme decorrelation can persist, particularly on the upside. ▪ Absolute dispersion for the late cycle: As the AI cycle matures, rising leverage and macro risks imply higher equity volatility. In late-cycle environments, the fattest tail in absolute terms is typically the right tail – for example, the Nasdaq-100's >100% rally from the first Fed rate hike in summer 1999 to the peak in March 2000. One of the most efficient ways to capture fat right tails in a decorrelated market is via a call on absolute dispersion: the "Talisman." This structure benefits from being a defined premium-at-risk trade and avoids the tail risk associated with a short index vol position. ▪ An attractive entry point: We have seen a significant unwind of the high-momentum trades that drove the fattest right tails earlier this year – such as US Semis and Korean equities. From a spot perspective, this provides an attractive entry point for many of the recent high-flying names. The volatility crush also presents an appealing entry point from an optionality parameter perspective. ▪ Screening for dispersion: One method to select names for a Talisman is backtesting, namely identifying optionality priced cheaply relative to historical return distributions. From 2005 to 2014, roughly two-thirds of presidential elections in the region’s largest economies resulted either in the sitting president being re-elected or in power remaining with a chosen successor. Re- election itself accounted for more than a third of those cases, with left-wing governments in particular retaining power for extended periods in Brazil, Argentina, Bolivia, Ecuador and Venezuela. In other words, siding with the current administra- tion or running for reelection looked like a positive. That pattern started to change over the following decade, as the positive impact of the commodity boom faded, and the most recent electoral cycle of 2025-26 largely reinforced the shift. Bolivia ended the political dominance of MAS, Chile returned the presidency to the right with Kast’s decisive vic- tory, and Colombia shifted from Petro’s left-wing administra- tion to De la Espriella.
